utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, interpreters and also the court reporters. Good morning to you all. I hope everyone can hear me. Let us now begin then and turn to Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next Defence witness is Vice-Admiral of the Croatian Army Davor Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think there is a transcript problem, seems that the format has changed. I see the characters are different now. I think this is a more modern system. Is that right, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, well for technical means, there is no reason to have another system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Has the system been changed?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. For technical reasons, we are required to be connected to a different system, which gives us this transcript for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Well, we'll do with what we have for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the screens on the video are virtually unreadable in my opinion. On the video monitor of the transcript. It's so faint you cannot read it. The laptop screen is quite readable. We have a laptop we have unplugged. I don't know if the laptop or more than one laptop can be brought to the Court. But we would like the Court to be able to see the transcript of this witness' testimony as it is given. I think it's an important aid, particularly given the translation. This witness will be testifying in BSC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Registrar, we don't have laptops. They have laptops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We can bring some to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it might be wise to provide us with laptops. I turn to my colleague, do you think we might go on as we are now into the break? Now we have nothing at all on the screen. The judges are ready to go on with the system until the break with the current transcript, which is even worse now I see. I am the least handicapped, but that's perhaps not the issue. Let us now go on with what we have now, but I am, nonetheless, going to ask that the witness express himself slowly and then after the break, I hope we'll have laptops by then. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps in the next 30 minutes the technical problem may be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo, now we have nothing on our screens at all. Mr. Nobilo, you may present your next witness. I wish to remind you, Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman, that pursuant to the recent decision on the presentation of a list of witnesses seven days in advance, that you are to make a summary. The Chamber is waiting for a written summary, not one of one or two lines, because that would not be very useful for us. Do you understand what I mean Mr. Hayman? Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I read the English version of the decision yesterday for the first time and we are studying it and we'll file a more detailed, if you will, statement on that, but we'll find our way and we'll look to the Court for guidance in that regard. THE COURT: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just make one comment on that. We also are handicapped in the course of preparing our examination of these witnesses because we also have received a one sentence topical summary of what these witnesses are going to say and we have not received a factual summary. We also have read the decision in English and in French. It is clear to us that what is required is a factual summary prepared and presented to the Prosecutor and to the Trial Chamber several days in advance. I have notified the Defence that that is your expectation and interpretation and we are waiting receipt of those factual summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter is not as simple as Mr. Harmon suggests. The Court can look at the testimony of this witness and ask itself, what should a summary of this witness' testimony be? We have advised the Prosecutor that this witness is going to testify concerning what the JNA's actions, strategies, in the wars in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, principally in the years 1991 and 1992. Now to go into the facts that he is going to present, either we describe the subject matter, the topic, or the Defence is going to be compelled to create some memorialisation of the witness' specific testimony, which, by the way, we do not always -- we have not always heard that seven days in advance. I heard this witness' presentation the day before yesterday for the first time. He was asked to prepare a presentation on a particular topic. I have never heard that presentation seven days in advance of today. So the Court is going to have to provide some flexibility and understanding for the Defence. We don't have a staff here. If the Court is telling Mr. Nobilo and I to take time out of the difficult preparations by the two of us, to prepare this case, to prepare a deposition transcript or a statement of facts of an individual witness, that is a serious matter, given the limited resources that the Defence has. So I suggest that the Court look at what we're filing, compare it to the testimony of the witnesses, we will work with Court. We will look to the Court for guidance. We will find our way. We wish to comply with the spirit of the Court's decision, but it is not a simple matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it isn't a simple matter because this summary that is now on the screen is different than the summary with which we were provided by the Defence on the 4th of September. I am sure, Mr. President, that the Court, if comparing this summary, if it is identical to the one we received, will notice that this summary is different than that which we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, I have never seen this slide presentation when under the Court's decision we were required to give a summary to the Prosecutor. That illustrates the problem of setting a calendar deadline by which we have to provide some kind of a statement of what a witness is going to say, when we may not have met with the witness, particularly experts, and heard the presentations that they have prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, the Prosecution and Defence. Here, first of all, one must apply the decision rendered by this Chamber on the 3rd of September, 1998. I understand that it may be a little delicate to try and interpret our decision, but, nonetheless, we are going to try and do so. First of all, I would say to the Defence counsel that I understand that the decision made on the 3rd of September, that the Defence was not able for this week to carry out exactly what the judges of this Chamber requested. As a consequence, for this week, that is to say for today and tomorrow, we will be content, we, the judges, will be content, and I will ask that the Prosecution also be satisfied, with what you have been able to present, given the lateness with which this decision was rendered on the 3rd September and the difficulty in which that put the Defence. Nonetheless, for the following week, that is to say for Monday, the 21st of September, we expect in its letter that the decision of the 3rd September will be respected. What did this decision say? Well, and I am turning to the Defence counsels now, we did not wish by this decision to impose all of the provisions within the 73 ter because these are obligations, which, as you understand, if you indeed correspond to -- or, the content, rather, of Rule 73 bis, which was not applied by the Prosecution. Nonetheless, since the rule is to be applied in the case, we, the judges, have requested what we felt appropriate to carry out these proceedings in good time. We have requested the names and the identifying information: name, place of birth, date of birth of the witnesses. This was requested within the described time limit. We have also requested a summary of the facts about which those witnesses will be testifying and that these be submitted. This summary in the process have been done verbally. Why? Because there have not been any text. But as of now, we feel that it is possible for the Defence to supply to the Prosecution and to the Chamber a summary of the facts upon which the witness will testify. In addition, we, the judges, we cannot and I think counsel for the Prosecution, but that is their own problem, but the judges cannot be satisfied with a single line summary. We're not going to ask you to write 15 or 20 lines or 30 lines, we simply wish that you respect the ledger and the spirit of this decision. We would like for a summary. Why? Because from that summary the judges will be able to ask questions and possibly interrupt you. All of this within the spirit of accelerating the process and the procedure. This is the spirit of the changes made to the rules of procedure in evidence. So we are not here to impose any obligations or have your obligations that we have already imposed upon the Prosecution. But we believe that having a summary on the testimony to be given by the witness is not too heavy a burden to impose upon you. Now, as for those trials which have not yet begun, this will be something that will be imposed on a regular basis. Here is what the ledger and the spirit of the decision was: Now, of course the decision was rendered on the 3rd of September; therefore, we will be satisfied with a verbal summary, which I believe Mr. Nobilo will present us with now. But, nonetheless, I think in the future, seven days in advance, we expect a summary, a factual summary, of what the witness will be testifying on and I hope that this will be relatively substantial. I think you understand there is a difference between one and two lines and a summary of several pages. I will not speak any further on this particular issue. I will now give the floor to Mr. Nobilo, so that he can present to us the testimony by this Vice-Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I have already said, our witness is Vice-Admiral of the Croatian Army, Davor Domazet, deputy Chief of staff of the main headquarters of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. The title of his expert report is as we see here, "The Role of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army and Serbian forces in the war in Croatian and in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Within the framework of his expert report and opinion, Admiral Domazet will discuss the transformation of the JNA into a Serbian imperial force. And on the preparations for the war on the soil of the republics of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina for the purpose of reaching the invented western border of Serbia. Secondly, the use of the defence plan of the JNA, co-named S-2, this is a defence plan designed during the era of communist Yugoslavia in the event of an attack by NATO. This plan from 1986 until 1990 was developed and it was on the basis of that plan that the JNA and Serbian forces were used in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also in Croatia. Furthermore, Admiral Domazet will present the strategy of so-called key points in Bosnia-Herzegovina which are a project of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. Fourth, he will describe the first stage of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the strategic level and also the control and command structure of the JNA and the Army of Republic of Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Fifth, he will present the command structure in the Army of Republic of Srpska after the alleged withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And sixth, describe the second stage of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina again from the strategic standpoint. Therefore, the admiral will be talking about the framework within which the conflict in Central Bosnia broke out between the Croats and Muslims. And this war of the JNA against Bosnia-Herzegovina as the backdrop had a decisive effect on the events we are discussing here. That is, the conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia. This expert report will clarify the disintegration of Yugoslavia and the key role played by the JNA in that process disintegration. And it will directly link up with the testimony of Professor Bilandzic. This testimony will significantly contribute to resolving certain dilemmas regarding the nature of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it will explain that Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia were treated by the JNA as a single theatre of war, which is correct from the strategic standpoint. Therefore, Mr. President, that would be a brief, oral summary of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I see you've taken a very good summary, Mr. Nobilo. This is the kind of summary that the Chamber would like to see that you are to disclose to the Prosecution. I see that your colleague is also congratulating you, Mr. Nobilo. I would also like for this type of summary to be given in French before the hearing begins. So that will be done in writing and in the future every judge will have a version in French or in English before him and this is something that will be presented before the entrance of the witness. Therefore, in the future, your examination-in-chief will be based on those issues covered in your summary. Therefore, now, Mr. Registrar, you may have Mr. Admiral Domazet brought into the courtroom. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will the usher please ask the witness to remain standing. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, will you please explain to the usher, once and for all, what type of protocol must exist in this courtroom. I do not wish to have to continue to repeat myself on this issue. Please have this explained to the witness beforehand. Mr. Admiral, do you hear me? Very well. Thank you for responding in French. Now, for the time being, I simply wish that you state your name, your first name and your rank and then please remain standing for the reading of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I am Vice-Admiral of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. My name is Davor Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the usher will show to you the solemn declaration, which you will read and then you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral, you may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Admiral, you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, the Tribunal thanks you for coming. You are here at the request of the Blaskic Defence, which is here before the International Criminal Tribunal in the case of Prosecutor versus Mr. Blaskic. You're now going to be answering questions put to you by the Defence. Please speak as freely as possible. Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As it is the rule here in Court, we need to introduce our expert witness to the Court, so will you please explain to the Court where you were born, which military schools you attended and your career in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of May, 1948, in Sinj in the Republic of Croatia. I graduated from secondary school of natural sciences in 1967. After that, I enrolled at the military naval academy, which I graduated from in 1971. After that, I sailed on boats very often as the commander of naval vessels. At the end of this period of sailing within the scope of the former navy of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, I was the commander of the Destroyer Split. In 1986 I was dismissed. And after that I became an analyst in the command of the navy, studying the NATO doctrines. In the meantime, I also completed a school of tactics and operations. This is a school for command officers. And in 1990, I attended the highest military school, the war school, which I abandoned three days before graduation, when the war broke out in Slovenia, or rather, when the JNA attacked Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left this war school three days before graduation, you joined the guards which became the precursor of the Croatian Army. What posts have you held in the Croatian Army to this day?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after leaving the war college, it is interesting to note that my trip from Belgrade to Zagreb was not a direct route, but I had to go through Sarajevo, Ploca Split and then Zagreb. The national guards, and these were yet the beginnings of the organisation of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. As a member of the command, I remained within the command throughout, but I changed positions. The first position I held was to organise the command of the headquarters of the national guards. After that, I was Chief of Staff in the department for strategic studies for the use of the Croatian Army. And as of 1992, I performed the duties of Chief of Staff of the intelligence department of the supreme command. And finally, as of 1996, I have held the position of Deputy Chief of Staff of the main command of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you have published dozens of papers analyses, reviews and articles in various specialised journals, you became a Counter-Admiral and a Vice-Admiral in 1998. We see the medals that you have on your uniform; can you tell us how many decorations you were awarded in the Republic of Croatia? And maybe you could mention those you consider to be particularly important.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have nine orders of merit. First, the order of Nikola Subic Zrinski for courage shown in war. Second, of Banja Josip Jelacic for successful command and control in the armed forces. A Croatian leaf for my overall contribution to the armed forces, another Croatian medal for honourable duty in the armed forces. I also am the bearer of a large number of medals for significant operations, Bljesak, Jefto, Oluja and an operation, if it can be called that, for the peaceful reintegration of the Croatian Danubian Region within the constitutional order of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the registrar to distribute the exhibits to facilitate following the testimony. I should also like the technician to switch on the monitors, the computer monitors. And perhaps could the lights be dimmed, too, so that visibility of the screen can be improved? Can we have the same slide we have on the screen on our monitors, please? INTERPRETER: Counsel is addressing the technicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vice-Admiral, in your own words, without much interference from me, could you describe to the Court what was the role of the Yugoslav People's Army and Serbian forces in the Croatian, and particularly in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, before I present my expert testimony on the role of the Yugoslav People's Army, or the JNA, and the Serbian forces in the war in Croatia and in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is my duty for the sake of simplicity to say that the entire presentation will be a multi-media presentation, as these are complex and specific military matters viewed from the strategic standpoint, and the aim is to make understanding easier. Secondly, there are three key terms that I will be using in my presentation. The first is an asymmetrical war, or a war waged when the technical factor is substantially different or more explicitly far beyond all military standards on the one hand, and very minimal or non-existent on the other. Second, strategy, because my presentation will be exclusively focused on a strategic understanding of the war. That is the approach which men of wisdom have long since adopted when defining war. Let me mention some. The well-known French theoretician Gaulfleur and Jaminee (Phoen); van Schlieffen; Willenhartdt; the American, and two unavoidable theoreticians Sonsuvo (Phoen) in ancient China, and also what is studied at all military schools, Clausewitz. Therefore, war cannot be observed, nor is it exclusively a military concept. A third term that I will be using less is tactics. That is the lowest level regarding the use of military force, either units or equipment. Having made those introductory remarks, I can proceed with my presentation. The starting point is 1985. We have before us ex-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: How were the armed forces of Yugoslavia organised at that time? First of all, it consisted of two components; that is, the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. So, it is an armed forces with two components. The JNA consisted of the military naval district, or the navy, marked in blue. The entire inland area of Yugoslavia was divided into armies at the highest level of command. It is important to note in this connection that the armies were military and territorial organisations, and not exclusively military organisations, which means that both in peace time and in war time they remain there. This is, in a way, an anachronism of contemporary military skills. Certain parts of those armies could be moved to the zones of responsibility of other armies. And the third component was the air force. If we were to look at the military and territorial division of the army, we will note immediately that the armies were, to a greater or lesser extent, more or less entirely covered the borders of the republics of Yugoslavia. They coincided with the borders. Therefore, the armed forces, as I said, consisted of two components, the JNA and the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence was exclusively under the responsibility of republican headquarters, which means that it was under the command of high military officials in the republics, and it was armed from the budget of those republics. Therefore, the overall conclusion regarding the state of the armed forces of Yugoslavia in 1985 was that the armies had republican characteristics. What about the national structure of army officers? That is the highest level of command of such armies. We have before us, Mr. President and Your Honours, the percentage share of officers as compared -- actually, that is the actual percentage of posts held by the various ethnic groups; but for the purposes of analysis, we have to see what it means in relation to the overall population, or rather the ethnic structure of individual republics. For the purpose of analysis, we have the index of disproportion. This index of disproportion shows, varies considerably, and it is 51 per cent in favour of the Serbs. With respect to the Montenegrins that index is 148; Macedonians 8; and a separate group that declared themselves to be Yugoslavs, for them the index was 45. Therefore, these figures coloured in blue show the disproportionate representation of certain groups in relation to others. Albanians 91 per cent, Hungarians 70, Croats 53, et cetera. What does this mean? It means that the disproportional representation was planned so that some ethnic groups were inadequately represented in the command structure. Therefore, in 1985 this national structure will change significantly when the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences was adopted in 1986. And when the new organisation of the armed forces was approved, and we will be discussing that in a few moments, then the total percentage of Serbs in the total number of officers exceeds 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, from the structure of the officers cadre prior to the war, conclude that at that time already the JNA, according to its structure, had become Serbian?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: We can conclude that, and we have an overall view of all the armies' officers. And if we add to this the fact that the commanding posts were predominantly held by Serbs, in my introductory address I said that in 1986 I was the commander of the Destroyer Split, and without any explanation I ceased to perform that duty. Thank you. And everything testified to the fact that I was a successful commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Therefore, on this basis, Your Honours, we will be able to see how the JNA became a Serbian imperial force. What did they do, in fact? First, the conclusion was that structurally speaking there should be more Serbs and less representatives of other peoples. This, as the basic principle, and the axiom, therefore, was that the JNA was an armed force of all the nations and nationalities in Yugoslavia, as they were called. And if that was the case, if that was the principle and the axiom, and a change of this kind set in, then it is very important, in fact, that that upon which the entire structure of Yugoslavia was based had now been disrupted. Second, the infrastructure had to be adapted to the deployment of forces following the plan of reaching the so-called western Serbian border. Third, in the organisational sense, that is to say not to have the organisation that prevailed hitherto, but a new one, and to adapt to the forces for the pacification of the territory before the Serbian political goal is made known, so, before that, to perform this organisational change in the JNA. Next, when we speak of the operative use of forces, this should be checked in extraordinary circumstances, and all this should be masked behind an alleged general aggression of NATO on Yugoslavia. Your Honours, here the essential points exist, and we should not use the armed forces of a country in this given circumstance. First of all, extraordinary circumstances; the armed forces will not be used for the defence of the integrity of that state by external jeopardy, but will be used for extraordinary circumstances, therefore, within that state, and we will agree that that is the task of somebody else; first of all, the police forces. And second, the NATO aggression in the 1980s, as we know full well, was a time of essential, main events that took place on the world scene. It was the time when Gorbachev and Reagan were holding negotiations in Reykjavik. That was the time when the United States of America were performing their operations of the El Dorado Canyon in order to punish terrorist actions in Libya. So, in this bipolar division of the world, for NATO to attack Yugoslavia, any strategist would tell you was unheard of. Furthermore, in implementing a plan of this kind in which the forces would be used for extraordinary circumstances, we must stress the Yugoslav option, therefore, that the JNA was fighting for Yugoslavia, and that to wait within for an internal enemy, this was a syntagma that that enemy should attack first and then should be destroyed. These are the words that General Kadijevic used in his book, "My Vision of the Disintegration" in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, let us make something a little more better known to the Court. Who was General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: General Kadijevic, at that time, he was the highest military officer in Yugoslavia, he was the Federal Secretary for National Defence, or for easier understanding, he was Minister of Defence, but he was a general, so, he had the function of command, supreme command. And the next thing that had to be done was to reshape the JNA into several Serbian armies with an accent on the defence of the endangered Serb population, which means that to turn one army into three armies, Serb armies. Your Honour, these six points were the guidelines which the JNA was to use and to become an important weapon in the strategy of the idea of greater Serbia, because the borders cannot be changed unless you have an armed force; or borders are changed, which history has taught us, exclusively through the use of armed force. Before us now we're going to have one of the key elements which will help us understand the war on the territory of Yugoslavia, or better said, in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, we are dealing with the year 1985. The idea on a reorganisation of the armed forces has been made public. How was this reorganisation put into practice? In front of us at this moment we have a new military and political division. Therefore, the army no longer exists, but what do we have in its stead? We have the military naval unit, which remains the navy, in the same, under the same competency as it had previously. But the essential changes took place on land, and in this case, let me repeat once again so that you can see on your monitors, on your screens, the first military unit, district, the first army district. And Mr. President, this can be seen on your screen, so this new army and naval district in which the command came from Belgrade incorporated a large portion of Croatia, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina; therefore, in the strategic concept of this division it can be called a great war field, battle field. And so, it is on this great battle field that everything that took place in the war later on happened. Then we have two other army districts, the third and the fifth, and you can see that they are much smaller and disproportionate, so, they have a peripheral role. In a structure of this kind in 1985 the changes lasted two years. So, one, the change was undertaken already in 1986, the memorandum was published by the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the reorganisation was completed in 1986. But the Serbian Academy of Science denoted the western Serbian border Virovitica, Karlovac, Karlobag, that western line. Therefore, it almost fully coincided with the great war theatre or the first field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, if we were to compare the western border which was proclaimed by the Serbian intellectuals in the Serbian Academy Virovitica, Karlovac, Karlobag; is that the same border which in the Second World War the Chetniks, Molvice denoted as the western Serbian border?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Not only Molvice, the border of a greater Serbia from World War II, but before that, the border with very slight deviations went along that line. The essence of that border is one, and that is how to take away from Croatia its waters, or how to take away from Croatia two-thirds of the Adriatic coast. And in that way, to completely isolate not only Croatia, but Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well. Therefore, the essential conclusion to be drawn here is that the new type of organisation for the JNA and its territorial division was a complete anachronism of military science and skills, and, Mr. President, as can be seen quite clearly, it has followed the borders on this large theatre of war upon which the whole situation was to evolve of later on. If we were to express this with a pseudo-mathematical formula, this would be none other than the fact that the first army district, plus the third army district, plus one-third of the fifth army district, plus two-thirds of the sea would be equal to a greater Serbia. And that is the constant element that will try to be implemented at beginning of 1990. We also see the relationship between land and sea, the ratio is five to one. Therefore, the war events would include the sea for a very small portion, whereas, the predominance of the war would take place inland, and the war would be waged for territory. What was needed for the JNA to become transformed into a Serbian imperial force? This had to be legalised in some way, and laws had to be enacted at the top level, and two laws of that kind were enacted. The first that you have already had occasion to view, which was the reorganisation of the armed forces in 1985, 1987, where there were no more armies, divisions and battalions; and instead of them, military regions were set up corps and brigades. I think it would be interesting to hear what I'm going to say next. The first call in the Yugoslav People's Army was set up in 1981. Your Honours, let's look at, it was set up in Kosovo. Why? Because that was the best organisation to pacify the region. And that model of the corps, of its set-up since 1981 exists up until 1985, that is to say, up until this reorganisation, served the purpose of an experiment of a laboratory sample. In Belgrade they concluded that if this sample was successful, if the experiment succeeded where 80 per cent of the population was non-Serb and we found that this was successful, there is no reason for this experiment not to be successful in the other regions of Yugoslavia where the (inaudible) for the Serbs were much better. When they were convinced this was so, they started the new reorganisation. However, another document was found to be necessary which would enable the armed forces to be used, deployed within Yugoslavia, or to find a legality for their use, for the use of the JNA forces in Yugoslavia. Your Honours, this second document, which on the 20th of May 1987, was adopted by the presidency was a strategy for total national defence and social self-protection. Nowhere in the world does a country have a strategic document of that kind. It is interesting to see what these two documents in fact mean, what they are based on. First, every republic, up until then, as General Kadijevic said, had its own army, and the commanders were, for the most part, from those republics. Second, the new division neglects the administrative borders of the republics. Therefore, Mr. President, here we have the essential word which is administrative borders, which is once again stressed by Kadijevic. That means that the top military officer in Yugoslavia determines what is meant by a border and what is not. So, as the top officer, he does not defend the constitution of Yugoslavia but in fact overthrows it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, Admiral, administrative borders, am I right in saying what Kadijevic had in mind there, the borders of the republics, therefore, Croatia, Bosnia and Serbia, he does not consider them to be republican borders but merely administrative borders?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true. And as Yugoslavia was a federal state, it implies, and there is no doubt on that question, that we are dealing with republican borders. And he does not recognise the federal set up of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Yugoslavia and the borders of the republics. Third, the operational development of the armed forces, therefore of the JNA, that they should be used according to extraordinary circumstances, not towards an external situation, but operatively to set them up for use in extraordinary circumstances. Furthermore, officers were brought who were strongly in favour of the idea of a greater Serbia and bringing them to the main command posts, regardless of their rank or of their professional skills for holding posts of that kind. Furthermore, the training should be structured in the, as they should be used following the new doctrine which the general staff called spatial conduct, and this was a separate use of the armed forces and we will talk about that later on. Once this had been completed and all the prerequisites were furnished for the JNA into a Serbian imperial force and what strategy is called a special strategy, that this army should be used to realise the ideas of a greater Serbia. Therefore, we can see that both documents contained these five provisions and a new force was created and its legitimacy determined for it to be used. In the implementation of such an enormous strategy as Bofar, the great theoretician would say, this is determined by military strategy and in this case it becomes dominant; whereas the other separate special strategies become less important. We can therefore draw the conclusion that military strategy and the use of force determined greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, what we see on our screens, the outline, that is the idea of a greater Serbia; is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, this is the concept of a greater Serbia according to the new military territorial division. And what they aspired to and the like motif was to remain present at all times. Military strategy, dominant military strategy, in this case, military strategy is now in the dominant, which means that territories can be one. Territories can be one and the population can be expelled from these regions. This military strategy had three basic foundations. We can see them on the left-hand side, left-bottom-hand corner of our screens. The first is the theoretical foundation; the second, the organisational foundation and the experimental foundation. The first theoretical foundation had in the spatial combat region -- or, a special warfare, had a distance impact. This doctrinaire organisation would be explained later on. Second: Organisational foundation. We have already seen this. This was the new reorganisation which was implemented from 1985 to 1986. And this brings us to the most important factor and that is the experimental foundation. Before us, Your Honours, we have the sign S-2. The sign S-2 was a war plan of the general staff of Yugoslavia, which meant and had the title of a radical aggression of NATO against Yugoslavia. Up until 1985, there was a war plan, which was denoted as War Plan S-1. And it meant a non-radical, but a partial aggression of the Warsaw Pact on Yugoslavia. Up until 1985, each year alternately, one or other training was in force for one or other plan. But, in 1986, only one form of training existed, the training for the S-2 plan and that was the radical aggression to counter the radical aggression against Yugoslavia. What can determine this war plan as being the strongest document was that each year, and that is understandable and it's done by every army in the world, exercises are held and training sessions are held. And it is indicative to note that on a top strategic level, there were exercises held according to the S-2 plan, both in 1986 and 1987 and 1988 and 1989 and 1990. And these exercises were termed Romanija. Your Honours, let me remind you that the Mountain of Romania was located next to Sarajevo. It was the code name between Sarajevo and Pale. And this was an indicative title given to the exercises, an indicative code name. Let us now, for purposes of understanding, take a look at what is meant by the doors of the great battlefield, the theatre of war. Let us look at the first military district. And let us analyse this along the coastal region for us to be able to determine the key points. Why is this important? We shall see that this is also linked up both in the war in Croatia and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What is important here? First, the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina lie, as you can see them, along the coast. We have before us and I repeat once again, we have towns. The most populated towns and areas. And it is in these large urban centres and towns, which was where there was predominantly a majority population of Croatian population. In those years we find the installations of the following JNA institutions: the commands, the military schools, logistic bases, military flats, offices, families of Serbian nationality, a large number of summer houses. And they were given loans, very favourable loans to build their summer houses which other people couldn't do. And then we had the political authorities, the party. Outside those towns there were two basic characteristics. And on this slide under A you had the stretch with a large percentage, a significant percentage, of Serb population. There was another belt encompassing the outer islands, outlying islands, where the JNA had elaborated navy strongholds with an important, well-organised military infrastructure, allegedly to defend itself from NATO. Both A and B, in fact, meant isolation for the main towns and urban centres along the coast. And if we look at the sandwich system, then we can see that it would be very easy to master this area and gain control of this area in the following way: To link A and B in points K. Mr. President, and Your Honours, points K were a constant, in which, from the aspects of strategy, you were able to govern not only Croatian regions, but in depth, the country in depth. These points K were from the Greek times, Roman times. At these points K it was the Roman legions which penetrated the interior of Aleria. By points K, the crusaders entered the territory towards Jerusalem. It is through points K that according to the ideas of planners in Belgrade, where we'll see later on, that the NATO forces were to enter allegedly for a radical aggression on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that we have completed what we wanted to say at this point. I think we are going to take a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree with you. Let's take a 20 minute recess now then. The Chamber stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor until 1.00 p.m., please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We stopped when you were speaking of the doors to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia as you called them. Could you explain to the Court why you called this the gate or the door? Could the lights be dimmed, please? Could the lights be dimmed, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the strategy, especially geo-strategy, and as I have already noted, when we go back into history in this area, the main point is not only the gateway from the Adriatic because it is the deepest sea in Europe. And it was the silk route that ended here too, the route that led all the way to China. In addition to a gateway, this could be called a gateway, a part of a gateway to Eurasia. And it is no coincidence that I have already mentioned that ever since Greek and Roman times, the crusaders, all great plans and even plans from the Second World War envisaged disembarkation of the allied forces because that would be the speediest way to penetrate into Europe, but also to go on from there into Asia. And that is why I call it that. In this particular case, it is the route leading to Bosnia-Herzegovina or out of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was speaking about the key points. These are those two key points: That is, the places where, if A and B are connected, one has control of the entire area. You are master of the area. And those two key points, constants, in simplified terms could be said to be Maslenica, and Slano or Neum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are two localities in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Let me repeat these two constants, which will be very important for understanding the relevance in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, a pseudomathematical formula says in order to gain control of these gateways or two-thirds of the military, naval area, one just has to have to have A, B and two Ks under one's control. Your Honours, you will now see the fundamental idea behind the war plan S-2 and the commanding staff war exercises, Romanija, which were held ever since 1986 and as far as 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, what we are seeing now, is that the original war plan of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, this is a copy. And in the left-hand corner, you can see a possible idea for manoeuvres of the Jadran Operative Group, which is the secret code name for the NATO, alleged and envisaged NATO, attack against Yugoslavia. So this is a copy of the original. If now we were to analyse this plan by means of a computer, we would get these two Ks and the belts A and B. In the right-hand corner, we see the idea behind the manoeuvres of operative group Jadran of the NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this original plan, which we see on the screen in the right-hand corner is being copied or superimposed over the computer drawing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, for the sake of understanding. According to this imagined NATO an attack, it would come from the Adriatic. And the bulk of the forces are linked to the tactical group Ancona. And then we have united NATO air forces, mostly of the United States under the command of the 5th. Then submarine forces and D minus 1, that is the day before the envisaged attack, aggression, those forces would come from the land to the Adriatic. And we have before us, the four assault naval groups, among which the UG-1 are Italian forces, UG-2 and 3, forces of the United States. And Assault Group 4 or UG-4 of Great Britain. And these forces are allegedly attacking Yugoslavia. D plus 2 is the day when a part of the forces are disembarking at point K.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An explanation, D plus 2, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: It means the second day of the beginning of the imagined aggression. This is a standard terminology used by all armed forces throughout the world. It is a standard for marking all war plans. So the forces are entering K at Slano. And then Day D plus 6, the bulk of the NATO forces are attacking K No. 2. That is Maslenica, Zadar, Ravni Kotari. And then on Day D plus 15, those same forces penetrate deep within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, the bulk of NATO forces would enter at points K-1 and K-2, as you can see marked on the screen now. So those are the key points. You have before you, Your Honours, a global plan, according to which the Yugoslav People's Army and Serbian forces carried out the aggression against Croatia in 1991. The operational basis, that is the buck of the forces for the aggression against Croatia came from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the territory from which the JNA would start its aggression against Croatia. The whole area of Croatia was divided into four parts. Once again, we see how the plan was executed regarding the advancement of forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and Serbian forces. Apart from the eastern part of Slavonia, where they came from the territory of Vojvodina or rather Serbia, all the other forces came from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the second stage, these forces, the forces from Eastern Slavonia, were to have linked up with the forces in Western Slavonia and thus reach the Western Serbian border. If we compare with this idea, the two already noted constants, point K we will see, and this will be demonstrated later, the identity between the plan for the NATO attack and this plan. The idea was to counter-attack points K, but, essentially, the idea was to occupy more territory. Such a strategic plan was applied in two stages. In the first stage, the role of the JNA was to capture key points. And the key points were Karlovac, Sisak, Pakrac, Osijek, Zadar, Dubrovnik and Vukovar. Marked on the slide in yellow. The JNA's task was to attack the main roads with combined infantry and tank units with artillery support and to hold those points and penetrate further inland. The role of the air force was to attack civilian objects and to destroy them in order to cause panic. And the role of the navy was to carry out a blockade. In the second stage of the implementation of this strategy, the plan was to simultaneously occupy a territory within those key points and to advance in a divergent manner in order to gain control of a large a territory as possible and to reach the Western Serbian border as quickly as possible. And then also at a lower level because this is a strategic level. At a lower level, and there were key points at the tactical level for capturing these areas. The tactics of the attack, Your Honours, though we are talking at the strategic level, is important to see how the area was pacified. First of all, bases had to be formed and those bases are no other than barracks in the Territory of Croatia. And the tactics, the same tactics was applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as far as we know now, also in Kosovo. Therefore, those bases are the barracks of the JNA, then villages and localities in which the majority population is Serbian or exclusively Serbian settlement, which had been armed by the Serbs. Then came the attack on Croatian villages, situated within Serb inhabited villages. The superiority of forces was 2-1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I apologise for interrupting, but I have a question to you to see whether we are of the same opinion. You said in Croatia, and I would add in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, one of the main characteristics was that the villages were military bases. And the villages constituted a kind of base for military units. One village; one military unit. Is my opinion correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct. The bases in addition to the barracks were the villages. Because they were armed, they were the bases on which military power could be based at a certain tactical level. Therefore, this 2-1 superiority in manpower and equipment, it was asymmetrical. So this is the term that I mentioned in my introduction, the asymmetrical war, that is a war between unequal opponents. A classical rule of warfare accepted in all the armies of the world is the balance of forces between the attacking forces and the forces of Defence should be 3-1. If one can talk at all about ethical warfare, then there would be some chances for the attacker and for the defence. However, in this case, not only in Croatia, but in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this superiority will be even more pronounced. It was not 3-1, but 100-1 or 1.000-1 because it was the armed forces that attacked unarmed people. The fourth point. In view of such tactics of attack, the artillery support, which was exclusively controlled by the JNA, was 10 kilometres in the rear, which meant a new kind of warfare, which is the distant attack, which has a twofold role. First, to provide fire support in the attack of ground forces, while, at the same time, cause panic and fire at villages. This principle, from the military standpoint can be described as a terrorist method, was also used in Croatia and particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina and as we can see nowadays in Kosovo as well. The logistics in such a concept of battle at the tactical level were trucks and helicopters. A general conclusion regarding such a deployment forces at the tactical level on the part of the Serbian rebels was to eradicate, chase out, destroy, the Croatian population. And this method of one Bosnia-Herzegovina meant the same to the Muslims and the Croats, resorting exclusively to terrorism and terrorist use of powerful military units. To gain a better understanding of the way in which tactics was applied from bases, we have a schematic presentation of an area along the edges of greater Serbia, where in the centre you have a city and in order to apply this special doctrine, one had to have control of the main communications. Then surrounding that city was smaller villages, and on the other hand, on the other side, were settlements and villages predominantly inhabited by Serbs as a base. And then also, it was necessary to link up with roads those localities. In this way, the territory can be covered without any major manoeuvring of forces. For such a battle in space to be carried out and to pacify such an area, close to the main city and at the main junction there used to be a barracks, if it was lacking it was built in the 80s, and then the weapons from that barracks was directed towards the city. Furthermore, for the entire territory to be pacified from bases with Serb inhabitants fire power was also positioned. Such a use of forces shows that no manoeuvring is required, and it is a kind of position deployment of forces and weapons, meant that its exclusive aim was to destroy civilian objects and facilities and this is particularly characteristic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that a village is destroyed that is outside that territory, so that space was captured in a relatively easy manner. This method of warfare was possible only because of the asymmetry that existed in equipment. What was the efficiency of the key points strategy? Your Honours, we have now before you a paradigm of the war which will highlight the significance of these gateways and perhaps provide an answer for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The date indicated is the 28th of September 1991, and the place is Ravno. Ravno, as can be seen, is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a locality exclusively inhabited by Croats. The JNA and the Serbs attacked it on that day and destroyed it on the 28th of September 1991. In their campaign against Dubrovnik, by destroying this locality, and because of a small depth of territory, Dubrovnik was cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use this operative depth, what does it mean in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to NATO standards, in its rules FM 105 of air and land battle, as part of the Doctrine of the Land Forces of the United States, it applies to a brigade as a tactical unit. It means that the area of responsibility of the brigade in defence is 35 kilometres, and the zone of interest for it to be effective is 75 kilometres. In this case that depth is only 800 metres. And where it is widest, it is not more than 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say 800 metres, do you mean to say that the width of Croatian territory from the Adriatic coastline to the Bosnian border is 800 metres, between 800 metres and 15 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that the operative depth of a brigade that would want to defend Dubrovnik could not defend it unless it enters the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe when talking about military operations one has to react according to circumstances, but any military expert will tell you that such a territory cannot be defended with such a small depth which ranges from 800 metres to a maximum of 15 kilometres, if you have forces that are using the whole depth of territory. Why? Because you can very quickly be cut off and you will lose all your forces. The price in manpower is vast. So, it is an immense challenge for any commander, and I would not like any commander of any national forces to find himself in such a position. Such a combined attack by the JNA and Serbian rebels along the main communication lines were relatively successful only in this area around Dubrovnik and not in other areas, because the Serbs, or rather the JNA, did not realise its plan to reach the western Serbian borders but managed to do so only in this area. The question is why. The answer has already been given; because, not only because Croatia at that time did not have the adequate weapons with which to resist, and even if it had, in view of this, its tactical position, it would be unable to do so from its own territory. But there is another important point here. If the JNA launched its attack on Dubrovnik on the 28th of September 1991 and attacked and destroyed a place, and when I say destroyed, I mean it in the literal sense, this meant that it was actually attacking Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I see that this is mentioned often, that it was then that the president of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina Alija Izetbegovic declared this was not his war. I have given the reasons why this was not successful. Let us now look to see what this idea meant globally, so we are coming to the end of the war in Croatia. The JNA and Serbia did not achieve its strategic goal, and its strategic goal, as Kadijevic said, was to defeat the Croatian army and to reach the Slovenian border, implying in fact, the western Serbian border. That was the time at the end of 1991, when Vukovar was destroyed and when actually the waters of Croatia were seized from it. Because from the strategic standpoint the war against Croatia was waged for two goals only, and those two goals were waters. The Danubian area, and as much of the Adriatic as possible. That is the crux of the matter and that is what Kadijevic actually said, that Croatia had to be moved away from the Danubian waterway. Croatia, or rather the main staff, had the following ideas in mind at the time: To continue the war in Croatia was unnecessary, it should be avoided. It was important to gain time, it was important to get, for the International Community to get involved. So, for a moment we will leave Croatia for a while and we will set up a new Serbian army which will be called the Serbian Army of Krajina, and all forces will be redirected towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if we manage to pacify Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather occupy it as quickly as possible, and according to some estimates, that was to have been done in seven days, then it will be easy to settle accounts with Croatia. And at that point in time Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes part of the game. Kadijevic will then say that without Yugoslavia there will be no state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What this meant was that the war in Croatia, the first part of the war in Croatia, and the war that was to follow in Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of one and the same plan. If we show this with a circle, we will see, as this cross shows in the middle, that the centre of that hole is situated somewhere in the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. From the standpoint of strategy, this meant that if this point is captured, then it will be easy for me to pacify Bosnia-Herzegovina. As on the 3rd of January a plan was signed on the entry of international forces, the UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean 3rd of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. International forces are deployed in this area that has been shaded in which the JNA and the Serbs had occupied. It is visible from this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, this territory is the territory within Croatia known as Krajina, mostly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not just Krajina. Actually only this part is known as Krajina. But under the name Krajina they called this para-state, the Serbian Krajina, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, which, according to them, also included the eastern part, which geographically does not connect at all. As you see, it is quite separate, they called it Krajina, as well. But this occupied territory can be linked only if Bosnia-Herzegovina is occupied, and that is part of the plan. That is why in 1992, from January until March, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the coming of international forces, the JNA corps are deployed. Mr. President, Your Honours, the manoeuvring of corps will best be seen on the monitor through animation. The first corps, the 31st Corps coming from Slovenia withdraws through Croatia and goes to Serbia, and passing through occupied territory, they leave most of the weapons to Serbs who are there. Then, applying the same methodology, the 14th Corps goes to Serbia leaving behind the weapons. Then the 14th Corps is redeployed to Montenegro. The manoeuvre of the 13th Corps is most noteworthy, it was situated in the area of Istria and Rijeka, that is the north-western part of Croatia, and across the Adriatic it will go to Bare to Montenegro and from there to eastern Herzegovina. A very important manoeuvre was that of the corps going from the occupied part of Croatia to western Bosnia. And the 9th and last corps, of which general Mladic was in command, will go to western Bosnia, which means it will come close to that point, if I may remind you of it, of the cross that you saw in the middle of the circle on the previous slide. At the time, within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these three corps were also deployed; therefore, one does not have to be a great military expert to come to the conclusion on the basis of this there were two groupings of forces; three corps in north-western Bosnia and two corps in south-eastern Bosnia, plus the corps which were deployed in Serbia and Montenegro close to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The commanders of those corps, and I don't want to read them, are the following: Of these names we will be able to note the commander of the 13th Corps in the south-eastern, that is to say in eastern Herzegovina, and at the time it was Major General Momcilo Perisic, who is a general now and head of general staff of Yugoslavia, Chief of Staff. The next we come to the year 1986. We're going back in time, now, to look at the plan and the Chief of Staff, the commanding staff of the war exercise entitled Romanija on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. President, we are now coming to the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Through animation we can see that is the imagined aggression of NATO in Yugoslavia which moves via Croatia, with the main force in key points K, are being extended and are entering into central Bosnia. How? First, with the breakthrough from point K, from Croatian territory, moving via the Neretva Valley towards Sarajevo. And second, from K 2, via Knin, Sinj, Livno, from the west towards Sarajevo. And now, a complete anachronism of war skills, but one of the key elements which would answer the question of why Sarajevo was encircled, as it was, and why Sarajevo experienced the atrocities of war in the 20th Century that it did, or at the end of the 20th Century. That meant that the American 101st Airborne Division in, according to this imaginative situation, would descend, Your Honours, on Mount Romanija. The 101st Airborne Division of the United States of America is a strategic unit within the composition of the forces of the United States of America. Therefore, in this absurdity that a complete division in a bipolar division of Europe, that the United States could not send this division anywhere else but to the mountain of Romanija. On this imagined operation by NATO, the JNA would have had to respond, and how was it to respond? Let's take a look. Your Honours, the JNA responded in the following manner: In addition to Sarajevo, the NATO forces were allegedly descended here, then we would have to have a semicircle in central and western Bosnia, and forces from Serbia and eastern Bosnia should move towards Sarajevo so as to break up the decent and to prevent it previously on this area around Sarajevo to organise a counter attack, assault. And in this, with this concept, since 1986 to 1992, the fate of Sarajevo was sealed. The second element meant that the forces from western Bosnia, which was the operative group around Kupres, should hit the flank with their forces which go from point K and come to the coast and organise a defence there. And third, operative group Mostar, for the NATO forces along the Neretva River Valley should be defeated and that the coast should be gained and defence set up there. Therefore, strategy at this point tells us that for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be defended from anybody in this case, from the JNA and from Serbia and the Serbs in Bosnia, this meant to defend the region of western Herzegovina, because land comes out onto the sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, can we clarify something here? I'm not clear, and perhaps Their Honours are not quite clear; you said the JNA thought up the possibility of a NATO attack, although there were no objective reasons for this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that direction, from 1986 up until 1990 they constantly held exercises, according to the model that we now have on our screens; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as there was no realistic reason to defend the territory from NATO, you wish to suggest that since 1986 to 1990 the JNA, in fact, prepared an assault on Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It preferred this attack, just as it did for Croatia previously. It was not a defence against NATO, because NATO in that situation could never have attacked. It was a model, the NATO model served for the operational development of the JNA in order to implement the occupation of Croatia first of all, and then of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the training of troops. Yes, every year. And that is why the Romanija code name for the exercises was given and took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly, then, that on this schematic representation we see first that the south Croatian battle field and the Bosnian battle field was, in fact, one battle field, and that therefore the key points for winning over Bosnia-Herzegovina were, in fact, near the borders of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, and that was not a strategic battle ground, but of a tactical, the lowest possible level, the south Croatian and the western Bosnian, yes, from the standpoints of operative skills and war skills. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The main point of the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the town of Sarajevo, and with this access point, how to occupy this as quickly as possible, it was necessary to occupy these, to capture these two areas. Why? Because we have the occupied areas of Croatia, which were under the control of the Serbian army and Krajina. So, the question that was raised and a comparative analysis will be made with slides to see the congruence between the manoeuvres of the war plan S1 and the operations which in the war were to evolve in the war in Croatia and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let us take a look. You can see, if we look at this picture better, it sort of associates with the state of affairs which was to occur in Bosnia. January-April, and the year is 1992. Therefore, we have before us, you have before you, Your Honours, the occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia. And what we see now is a regrouping of the JNA in such a way that on occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia, a new Serbian army is deployed, the army of the Srpska Krajina Republic, to retain what was won, and the JNA is reorganised in the following manner. You have in front of you four new military districts. Those military districts had the following strength: The first was in Belgrade, and its cause, its organisation, in fact. The second was positioned in Sarajevo; the third was from Skopje transferred to Nis; and the fourth was in Podgorica, Montenegro. That is the new military and territorial division, the new set-up that was made after the signing of an agreement on the 3rd of January 1992, and with the arrival of the international forces in Croatia for Bosnia-Herzegovina and the remainder of the former Yugoslavia. These forces at that time, the JNA forces, were of the following strength: Before that we can see the national composition, not only of the command structure but of the entire armed forces. The command structure, as I say. Serbs almost 93 per cent; Montenegrins 7 per cent; and the others not .4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said 4 per cent, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not .4 per cent, yes. Therefore, we may conclude that at that time the JNA and its complete commanding cadre was Serbian. At that time it was located in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was not an armed force of the other two peoples. The strength, if we were to analyse strength in Bosnia-Herzegovina alone, it was as follows: 83.000 men, between 460 and 500 tanks, 400 to 420 armoured vehicles, and about 1.000 guns, artillery pieces. This new organisation and the system of command in the first phase of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was as follows: The commanding officer of the SNO and general staff, no longer General Kadijevic, but it was now Lieutenant General Blagoje Adzic, who at the same time performed the function of federal secretary. So, at that time he was also the Minister of Defence and the Chief of Staff of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The commander of the second military district, that is to say in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was Lieutenant General Milutin Kukanjac. The heads of the 4th Corps of Sarajevo commanders were General Bojislav Durdevac; of the 5th Corps of Banja Luka, Major General Vladimir Vukovic; the 9th Corps of Knin was Sava Kovacevic, and his Deputy or Chief of Staff of the corps was Major General Ratko Mladic. The commander of the 10th Corps in Bihac was Major General Spiro Ninkovic. From the 1st Army District, from the region which is Serbian Belgrade and Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the 17th Corps under the command of the General Sava Jankovic. And the 4th Army District, therefore, this was Montenegro, was the 13th Corps under the command of General Momcilo Perisic. This structure of command after the resignation or dismissal of general of the army (inaudible), that was never determined; his duties were taken over by General Blagoje Adzic. Apart from that, here we can see one more factor, and that is that for the commander of the second army district, General Kukanjac, that is to say the territory of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were forces deployed of the 9th, 10th and 13th Corps, which came from the region of Croatia. Let us now try, Mr. President and Your Honours, to have a look. I'm going to try and show why this kind of military territorial division was affected. And I am showing you that now. The second army district, which is located on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, naturally continues on from the occupied areas of the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, and in that region already, the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina is already deployed. On some letters, say Western Serbia border, which after the war in Croatia was as it stood. And not only that, in its southern portion, it extends towards the responsibility zone via the territory of Croatia to the Adriatic Sea. The fourth army district and there links with the first army district, naturally tends towards Split and outwards towards the sea. Another important factor is the following: The second army district, which is located on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina must -- we must add that the first army district crosses the River Drina and enters Bosnia. And this is a very significant factor in order to compare forces in the first phase of the war. And second, that the fourth army district, which has a small operative debt is increased by entry into Serbia army. So this division of forces is achieved in two ways. First of all, it covers the whole area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And military power can be projected towards Croatia, across Croatia. At that time, if this area is gained one over, then you will have the capture, then you will have the borders of greater Serbia. And it is not Vidovica, Karlovac, Karlobag, but it is not very far from that. It goes along the line of Maslenica, Nis, Karlovac, up to Sisak, by the Sava River, to Vukovar which is already occupied and destroyed, up to Vinkovci and Osijek. Therefore, at this point in time, if Bosnia was pacified, one would get a greater Serbia. What is the key to capturing as fast as possible and to breaking down any resistance in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Let us recall what the two key points are: The key points are, therefore, this part of Herzegovina. That is the constant to two Ks and the capital, Sarajevo. And the first phase of the war, with this kind of distribution of forces is based, Your Honours, begins, Your Honours, in April 1992. That is the situation in April 1992. Once again, we have some animation here. According to the concept and the exercises that have been ongoing for six years on the western part, the operative group Kupres and the south eastern part with an operative group entitled Mostar, in this area, was to close up the territory. The whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that point, had the JNA succeeded in closing the pincer, then the entire region of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been isolated. It was separated. And after that, there was to be the liquidation of the capital city, because, let me remind you that at that time, already Sarajevo had already been encircled. And according to the concept of five years of exercise and training, and to defend the descent by the 101st Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we dwell for a moment, please, Admiral, on this point in time. When you say to close the pincers, why should this for Bosnia and Herzegovina and the non-Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is for the Bosnian Muslims and Croats for the defence from the JNA, why would it have been a very bad thing had they lost their inland link with Croatia? What did Croatia mean for them? Why would this have been fatal? What did Croatian ports mean for the survival of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we look at the situation, then we see that the occupied regions of Croatia have two basic characteristics: First of all, Croatia was cut across along its coastal lines, which was very important and traffic evolved only via one destroyed bridge. This is the Island of Pag which links the coast with the mainland. And the JNA in the war in Croatia in 1991 seriously damaged the bridge, so that traffic was very risky and overall traffic between the northern part of Croatia, moving towards the southern portions of Croatia, which is seen here, went via that particular bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about traffic towards Bosnia and Herzegovina for the non-occupied parts, for the needs of the Bosnian Croats, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The overall transport links and supplies for the population went via this free territory between Slano and Sinj. And it went from that territory, which means that it went from Split towards Sarajevo and Tuzla. That was the only communication line. And the only communication line which meant the difference between life and death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Admiral, whether the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina could have received a single bullet without that bullet passing via the Republic of Croatia, whether through the mainland or through the sea links?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, that was the only communication. And that is why the Serbian plans that we saw earlier on denoted this as being a key point. For that reason, in the expert report that I am presenting before this Court, I have emphasised the key points. And strategy teaches us just one thing and that is they were ideas of the great theoretician, who was Churchill, in fact, said this in the eloquent way that he always did. He said from defeat to victory. And when he said defeat, he meant tactics. And victory, and when he said victory, he undermined strategy. So, in this particular case, from the strategic standpoint, this communication line which went down the coast and across the mainland towards Croatia, meant survival for the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Another thing that I mentioned is the following, the asymmetry of the war, of the Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats, they did not have weapons. They were in a far worse position than was the case in Croatia. Why? Because Croatia managed to get weapons by attacking barracks when the aggression started. This was not the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina because the JNA had learned its lesson in Croatia and organised operations in a different way. And the only communication line was the line that I described. And in the case of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was to prove correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Therefore, at this point in time, the first phase of the war, Serbia and the JNA, did not succeed in realising its strategic plan, which was to close the doors, to close the gateway. Nor was the capital, Sarajevo, at that time, captured. And it was at this point --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to interrupt you once again to ask you why it did not succeed in closing the pincers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Because the defenders succeeded in refuting the attacks; one from the area of Kupres, via Livno, towards Split. And the second line was to move towards the right banks of the River Neretva and join there and a second direction via Eastern Herzegovina towards the Neretva River. Which means that the main battle in which the defenders succeeded in stopping the advance, both in the Luvansko-Kupreski (Phoen) part and in the Neretva region, Mostar, Stolavi (Phoen).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Luvansko-Kupreski and Mostar Stolavi, those, in fact, are geographical concepts from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, geographical concepts in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, exclusively. At that particular point, Your Honours, there were a lot of polemics as to whether Croatia could have in 1991, defeated Serbia, the Army of Yugoslavia. All reports showed that it just could not have done that.
