It succeeded in winning the first phase of the war, exclusively, strategy tell us, because it stopped these Serbs from realising their strategic plan. That is, to emerge along the western borders. And strategy in this area at this particular time in the first phase of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina shows that at that time the Serbs Clausewitz was the strategy key point, the culmination, the peak, was when one side in the war reaches its peak. At that time, it failed to close the pincers and so Serbia and its imperial force, the JNA, had reached their peak and, at that point, they were to change their tactics. And so, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was altered and took on different connotations which I am going to tell you of later on in my presentation. Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have a little problem, I wonder if you can help me. The admiral points with his pointer to a certain point on the map. And, quite naturally, he continues to speak. And while he continues to speak, the pointer is still pointing to different places on the map. Now, my mind, which is rather slow, continues to be attracted by the point on the map, which no longer has any relevance to what he is saying. Is there some way that you can resolve the problem for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you're quite right. The admiral is a man of temperament and while he talks, he moves his hands about. So we'll ask the admiral, if he will, to pinpoint exactly the position he wishes to illustrate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a slight problem here with my laser beam, my laser pointer. There is interrupted action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, of course we're going to take a pause here. But I have a slight problem myself, but of course you're the master of your own schedule, your own time. I do not have the written summary. Of course I will have it in the future, which will make this more sufficient. But I want you to truly focus in on your objective. We are here dealing with a time in the war, which I am sure for you has routes in the earlier phases of the conflict. But, nonetheless, I would like for you to take advantage at the time at lunch, to find how you can focus us progressively into what should be the most important point of the charges against your client. Thank you very much, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I am just getting to that phase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, we will all have lunch and come back for 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us now resume. Admiral, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you been able to rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sometimes it is difficult, I imagine. Let us now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let us resume, and I believe we will be done in about 20 minutes, that is with our direct examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, we stopped with the first phase of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina when a good basis was established for the subsequent resistance against the Serbian aggressor by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first characteristic of the first phase of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the halting, or rather the prevention of the closing of the circle or of the pincers, which actually would mean the total occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what I'm referring to. And this was the end of April, 1992. At that point in time the headquarters, the supreme command changed the decision and the JNA had to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then it took a new decision to reorganise a new Serbian army which was to continue the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina until 1995, or until the Dayton Agreement. We are now talking about the month of May, 1992. At the time there were, in fact, three Serbian armies which acted in line with the screen play long since established, that is, some six years previously; that was the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Serbian Army of Krajina in the occupied area of the Republic of Croatia. These three armies were under a unified command of the general staff of the JNA in Belgrade, and at the strategic level they had two tasks. The first was to coordinate the production of defence plans, and the second to protect the external borders and their integration into the system of Yugoslavia. Under that term they implied the occupied parts of the Republic of Croatia and the largest possible part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The command structure which they left behind in Bosnia-Herzegovina meant that on the 10th of May 1992, Lieutenant General Blagoje Adzic issued an order when General Milutin Kukanjac was being held in captivity in the JNA centre in Sarajevo. The command read as follows: We can see that the structure at the highest level of command in the Army of Republika Srpska was determined, the commander of which was Lieutenant Colonel Ratko Mladic. That was when the JNA was reshaped into the Serbian Army of Republika Srpska. The commander became Ratko Mladic, the Chief of Staff General Manojlo Milovanovic. The previous 5th Corps of the JNA was transformed into the first Krajina Corps. The 9th and 10th were transformed into the second Krajina Corps with their own commanders. The 17th Corps remains the eastern Bosnian Corps with its commanders. And the 4th Corps is transformed into the Sarajevo Romanija Corps with its own commanders. And a new corps actually consisting of the forces that stayed behind on the left bank of the Drina River that is within the territory of the Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Drina Corps. And finally the 13th Corps, which was renamed the Herzegovina Corps. Such a command structure meant that the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia was actually just declarative, whereas the command structure, the appointment, promotion, payment and planning of forces remained within the exclusive competence of the general staff of the army of Yugoslavia. Your Honours, on this slide, one that I consider to be very important for this Court, we will see the distribution of the new Serbian army within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is important because we will see from it what its role was in 1993, '94 and '95. This is the area held or controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska at this point in time, and we see this area which was actually under the control of the emerging army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. At this point in time we can see that virtually 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the occupation of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, could we now go back to the pincers you were talking about? Where was the attempt to close them halted?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the left end, in the area of Livno and Kupres, that is one of the prongs of the area and the other is the area of Mostar Stolovi. So, this is the gateway that will, in the next phase of the war, enable the survival of this whole area right up to the north-eastern part of Bosnia. The disposition of the Army of Republika Srpska and its cause was as follows, in terms of strength: The eastern Bosnian Corps covered this area, in terms of territory. The Drina Corps covered this area that I'm showing now, marked in pale blue. Then the Herzegovina Corps occupied this area here. It covered this area with its forces. The next and most important for this Trial Chamber is the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which had responsibility over the whole City of Sarajevo, as well as the central part of Bosnia. The area was covered by these forces. Then, the second Krajina Corps, which was deployed here from Bihac to Livno and Kupres, and the last and largest in terms of strength and territory was the first Krajina Corps which controlled the northern and central part of Bosnia. Such a disposition of forces meant that there were three areas which territory-wise were not within the responsibility of any of those corps, and those are the three areas which were preserved either thanks to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the west or east, or jointly, at least in the first stage of the war, by the HVO and the BH army here. Even though the central part of Bosnia where the 1930 events took place was also under the control either of the BH army or the HVO, such a disposition of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps meant only one thing, and that was that in the next stage of the war they would try to conquer this central part, as well. And if they were to manage to capture this central part, it would mean it was just a matter of days when the north-eastern part would be captured. After that it would not be too difficult to deal with the western part and eventually and finally also deal with the problem of the gateway to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, Your Honours, such a disposition of operative forces in 1993 meant that the Serbs had at their disposal 135.000 men, 550 tanks, 430 armoured vehicles, and more than 1.300 artillery weapons. And it also meant that in the second phase of the war, which from the standpoint of strategy is considered to be the period from 1993 until 1995, until the operations when the BH army and the Croatian forces managed to liberate the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which also made possible the Dayton Agreement. In view of the fact, Your Honours, that the Serbs had lost much of their attack strength, they applied a new kind of strategy which was designed in the general staff, and it was first applied in the occupied areas of Croatia, and then in an even harsher form in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was known as the strategy of real threat. That strategy meant to hold the positions that you have; but close to those borders, close to those borders deploy as many artillery pieces and rocket launchers, and then through constant action create a psychosis, which occurred as a result of large scale resettlement from the north-west into central Bosnia, from the east to central Bosnia, where there was the highest concentration of either Muslims or Croats. This strategy of real threat at this point in time, that is in 1993, meant waiting for the process of conflict to occur spontaneously between the Muslims and the Croats. May I, to illustrate this, use a very nice African proverb which says "When elephants fight, then it is the grass that suffers." In this case one can make an inversion of this proverb. At this point in time, the Serbs who have the strength and the superiority lying in wait, the International Community is not reacting adequately, and it was the grass in central Bosnia that suffered. But this meant that before the eyes of the world, a process was evolving in which such atrocities as the attack on the Merkale Market occurred. Within the framework of this strategy of waiting for the process to develop of its own accord, it was applied until 1995. That is, as I already said, until joint operations were launched and which managed when more than 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia was in the hands of Serbs to reduce that percentage to less than 47 per cent, and this also led up to the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, let us stop there for a moment to check that we understood you well. So, it is your opinion that the Army of Republika Srpska and the former JNA moved the non-Serb population from eastern Bosnia and Bosnia Krajina to central Bosnia, and that was one of the main detonators of the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, and that was part of the strategic plan of the Army of Republika Srpska; have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. From eastern Bosnia, which had been dealt with by the Serbian army gaining control over it, a large percentage of the Bosnian Muslims were chased out to central Bosnia. The same applied to a part of northern and western Bosnia. But from this area, from the northern part, there was a large influx of Muslims or Bosnians, as well as of Croats, to central Bosnia. So that on this very limited space there was a large number of people, and the only situation that can result from this was chaos. Because, as you can see, it is literally closed in from all sides, the northern, the eastern and the southern, and all that remains is this narrow corridor leading from south-east to the centre of Bosnia. And if we add in to this new strategy of real threat artillery to a greater or lesser extent, but continuously, the negative psychosis would develop and would eventually lead to what indeed happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any further comments about this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that no further comments are required regarding this map, but there is something that I need to emphasise. There were three key elements of the attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina. First, the joint action of Muslims and Croats in the first phase of the war when they prevented this circle to be fully closed in the fall of Bosnia. Secondly, from the standpoint of the Croats and Muslims, that chaotic situation in the central area occurred. And third, joint action in strategic offensive operations to liberate occupied areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say by way of conclusion of the first part of your testimony that the analysis of the restructuring and reorganisation of the JNA shows that the JNA was gradually transformed into a Serbian imperial force designed to establish the western borders of greater Serbia far before the democratic changes in Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia; would that be a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is an absolutely correct conclusion. Talking from the level of strategy on the global level one can make three basic conclusions. First, that the JNA was restructured into a Serbian imperial force before the Serbian political goal was made public, before Milosevic appeared on the political scene, and far before any new authorities in any republics were installed. That is my first conclusion. Second important conclusion is that the operational base in the southern part of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was such that from the military standpoint it constituted a unified operative hole. It is not possible to defend any of these areas unless they are defended integrally. And a third fundamental conclusion that may be drawn is that under such extremely complicated and unfavourable operational positions that both the BH army forces and the HVO forces found themselves in, the only possible logistic support could be obtained through this naval and land route leading from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is, those are the strategic conclusions on the global level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I thank you, may I ask you another very direct question, theoretical question? If Croatia had decided to defeat the BH army, could it have done so very simply by cutting off the route of supply, and would that have been the end of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, my direct examination is over. Mr. President, my colleague, Mr. Hayman, has reminded me that we would like to tender this set of maps shown on the monitor into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any particular comment, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you give it a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be 182 for the entire group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar, Mr. Cayley. Admiral, you will now receive questions from the office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Cayley. Cross-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Admiral. My name is Cayley, these are my colleagues, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Kehoe. I have a few questions for you. Now, I want to make sure that I actually understand this plan that you were speaking of. In essence, what I understood you to say was that in the mid-1980s the JNA general staff transformed a defensive plan against NATO into one of offence within Yugoslavia in order to create a Serbian state within that geographical area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have come up with your conclusions by drawing inferences from events which occurred on the ground in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you published this theory in any formal publication?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, in several publications. I think two. In a professional military journal, Hrvatski Vojnik is the name of the journal, but not in the integral manner, but it was published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the second journal in which you published this theory?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was another publication, but they were two studies. One described the war in Croatia and preparations in Croatia, and the second in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, it was the same publication and two articles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what period in time did you make your final conclusions about this theory of Serbian aggression?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The conclusions, I came to these conclusions in time. First of all, because I was in a possibility to -- I had the opportunity of knowing, conditionally speaking, the eastern school of thought in military thinking, the JNA and everything which was a projection taken over from the Red Army, because it was based on the heritage of that army. And secondly, because for five or six years I studied NATO's doctrine. Also, because I was at the war college in Belgrade and some of the elements were used at the war college. Third, because in the military naval region I took part, I was in the command which prepared the exercises for Romanija. So, that was my starting premise. Secondly, there was my own participation in the war from 1991, and I followed that theory and saw how and to what extent it would evolve. Therefore, the conclusion is that it was a systematic follow-up on the basis of knowledge and experience. I wrote my articles in 1996 relating to this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the article that was published in Hrvatski Vojnik was published in 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: One for Bosnia and previously for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have copies of that article which you wrote for Hrvatski Vojnik, and if we can take a moment to look at it if you can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the usher could assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 466.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I must apologise to the Court, I don't have an English or French translation, not an official English translation. I only anticipate referring to very limited segments of it, and I think they are such short segments the Admiral can read them to the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, is this the article which you wrote for Hrvatski Vojnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 7 of that article and the final paragraph on page 7, and could you read that paragraph to the Court, please? It begins --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: "Defence of the south-western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina meant at the same time salvation not only for Bosnia and Herzegovina but for the whole of southern Croatia as well".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, I'm correct in concluding from that comment that the pincers that we referred to earlier closed, the whole of southern Croatia would have been lost; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the first case this means, and I think that I have already explained this, that at that time there would be no more Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that it would mean the following: So, no more Bosnia-Herzegovina, the southern part of Croatia was isolated completely, and then this would be directed towards Croatia in a subsequent phase of the war. Now, how Croatia would defend itself, that's another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in terms of preventing these pincers from closing, the Republic of Croatia had a strategic interest of preventing that from happening, as well as the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, it did have because then, not only the southern part, but the entire Republic of Croatia would have been incorporated and lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to turn to the next page, which is page 8. And I think it begins -- I apologise for my pronunciation. Can you read the first four lines of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. As the efforts of the JNA for Bosnia to be defeated, the selective use of military force did not give off the results expected. First of all, with the Croatian people who had organised themselves militarily and was directed towards the correct realisation of the pacification of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the Croatian model. Which, because part of the Bosnian Muslim leadership, by waiving had strengthened the conviction with the JNA that the war would end very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you referred to that earlier when you said that, in essence, that Alija Izetbegovic wavered about taking any action against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, we can say that. And that is a conclusion with Ravno. That is, during the war in Croatia on the 28th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of that paragraph, you state that the JNA's efforts in Bosnia did not yield results, especially with the Croat nation, which was militarily organised. Are you referring to the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mainly I am speaking about the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've finished with that. Thank you very much, Admiral, and I apologise for my pronunciation. Now, you spoke in your examination-in-chief that one of the aims of the JNA was to win territory and expel the population. Now, by that, are you referring to what commonly became known as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not in that sense. As an officer, I don't work as such, but as military operations are under way, then they're freed and the population leaves, departs. Officers do not use the term ethnic cleansing, at least I don't use that term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If this map could be placed onto the easel, actually it's not a very big easel, it's a big map, but we'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I get up closer to the map? It's rather a long way off and I can't quite see. May I approach the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Admiral, Mr. Nobilo was asking you earlier and we sort of glided over this subject about the necessity in narrow areas of land mass for depth of forces. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. And I stated American Rules FMs 105 that this depth is 35 kilometres for effective and efficient defence to be set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about the very narrow coastal strip where Croatia, I think, is no more in some places, no more than 1.000 metres wide from the coast to the Bosnian border?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, between 800 to 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the defensive action against this pincer movement, you would accept, Admiral, that elements of HV forces were deployed in the border land areas of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As this was at a tactical level, which is not the subject, was not the subject of my research, but the subject of my research is strategy, I cannot answer that question. Second, for me to answer it, I would have to have an authorisation by the Minister of Defence of Croatia. And the authorisation I have is the expert report on the level of strategy, the one that I presented to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Admiral, you, yourself, fought in Livno, didn't you, with the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, I did not fight in Livno. Your Honours, it would be important for us to show you where Livno lies. Livno is located here. And my native town is there, which means that, at that time, I was in the command for strategic research. Your Honours, I am now going to digress somewhat in order to answer the question put to me by the Prosecutor completely. At that particular time, the Serbs held under occupation, the electric power plant of Pedajar (Phoen). This is on Croatian territory. It is located here. They were threatening to destroy the dam and flood or everybody south of that line, which would mean almost 100.000. On the other hand, in this area of Livno here, another lake is located and another electric power plant, hydro-electric power plant, which is called Busko Blato. The characteristics of that power plant is very interesting. The lake is on the Bosnia-Herzegovina side. That is to say, in another state. And a tunnel, across the border, through the Kamesnica Mountain. There is a great tunnel there. It's 20 kilometres long. And the hydro-electric power plant is on the Croatian side. Therefore, if at that time, the power plant were taken over by the Serb forces, this would mean that practically the whole of Croatia would have no electricity, the southern part, and that would be an end to the situation. But there is another case. This tunnel, which, as I say, is 20 kilometres long, was constructed in such a way that the electric power plant can be stopped and tanks can pass -- and this is interesting -- through this tunnel and emerge into Dalmatia. And then, this dam would be used as an additional element of terrorist use, use for terrorist destruction, not only of Dalmatia, but of this region of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. In strategic considerations, there is a very legitimate action and that is preventative defence. It is referred to as preventative defence, which implies a struggle against all terrorism, launching cruise rockets, tomahawks, in the Sudan, for example. And in Afghanistan, meant preventative defence against terrorism. And, at that particular time, to an allow the Serbs, I say the Serbs, and to do that, that would have been a catastrophe. So it was up to every honourable man to combat terrorism. He must stand up to terrorism and that was my role there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, it's not a criticism of your role in the war. And the fact that Livno was defended. So, I'd be right in understanding that the HV did deploy into Livno to secure that area to prevent this military terrorism?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, you asked whether I was there. And I said why I was there. The reason for being there, not as distribution of forces, but the importance that that area had. So you ask me personally and I said the reasons for which I was there, for the following reasons, the ones I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period of time was the HV deployed inside the Bosnian border?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an objection. Admiral Domazet is a member of the Chief of Staff of the Croatian Army. And in keeping with the laws on military secrets, every officer, active duty officer, must gain written authorisation from the defence minister if he is to disclose these facts and declassification of these facts and he be allowed to present them to the public. Admiral Domazet has received authorisation to present the strategic level, which is completely different from the tactical level. So the actual use of units in combat activities. And a few minutes ago, he stated what his legal authorisations were and what the obstacles were to answering this question. So, as we are dealing with a matter of state security that these questions be banned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a question to ask. Mr. Nobilo, this witness was presented by you, but he was not accompanied by any particular request for protective measures. For example, under Rule 70. Under these conditions, are you saying that the Chamber itself may not ask any questions itself on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are legal provisions binding this witness and if he were to violate them, this would be a criminal act. I am convinced that this Trial Chamber will not compel the witness to perform a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. But, you know, in principle, Mr. Nobilo, that the witness must answer all the questions put to him and especially by the judges. We have had witnesses who have appeared under particular protective measures. Please recall that there are very sensitive issues under Rule 70 in the rules. And the admiral is here before us now. He is testifying publicly, freely. He is now being subjected to a cross-examination, which, perhaps, may not please you with regards to the lines that he is following now, but it is quite important and so this is a very delicate issue. But what kind of response will the witness give us if the judges were to ask such questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, you can probably ask, but it is my view that the national security is legally binding and with the threat of a criminal act. And this is a legitimate right to which the witness can refer. As the witness has already spoken about the strategic level, a tactical level is quite a different area of expertise and outside the focus of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think there is a very subtle difference between the strategic and tactical. In my own language, I think that the two are quite similar. I would like nonetheless to consult with my colleagues because I think this is a very important issue. Please note the fact that the witness is here before us now. In your opening statement, Mr. Hayman, and also in the indictments issued against Mr. Blaskic with regard to the armed international conflict, it stated quite explicitly, here I am referring to the interference, opposing interference or alleged interference of Croatia in the events. So this bothers me to some degree. Because it does so, I am going to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are rules on this question. Just so that the Court, perhaps, has in mind, rules such as Rule 66 (C) and Rule 70, which the Court has stated applies to the Defence in this case. There is precedent and guidance, we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I would like to consult with my colleagues, but indeed Rule 66 (C) deals with disclosure of evidence by the Prosecutor. First of all, the Defence did not request any protective measures under Rule 70. Secondly, Rule 70 and 66 (C) is not applicable in the present case. Thirdly, it is true that Rule 70 (F) does indeed allow a witness to refuse to testify on the grounds that he might be incriminating himself. But the judges deem this is incrimination before the Trial Chamber, which has jurisdiction in that matter. Fourth, the Trial Chamber authorises the Prosecutor to put one at a time, the questions he wishes to put to the witness. Fifth, the witness may respond as he wishes. He may not respond if he chooses to do so, but the Prosecutor shall evaluate the value of that response, the weight of that response. The Tribunal shall weigh the value of that response. The Trial Chamber, rather, shall weigh the value of that response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, what I would like you to do on the map next to you is to draw a line indicating to the judges in the time period of the beginning of 1992 to the end of 1993, the outer limit of deployment of HV forces into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As this is a tactical matter, it is not the subject of my research. A tactical deployment of forces is separate from strategy. As an officer, I repeat, I do not have permission to speak about something that is not within the field of my research. Therefore, I have no permission by the Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, were the units of the HV deployed into Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As I was performing the duty of Chief of Staff of the Intelligence Administration, Intelligence Department of the main command, that was not within the field of my activities. I repeat again that I do not have the authorisation of the defence minister to make any such statements. And that is the duty of any officer to respect that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're stating that whilst Chief of Military Intelligence, you had no knowledge about the deployment of Croatian armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that's what you're saying to the judges?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I wish to say that the Chief of Intelligence, his responsibility is to monitor the forces of the enemy, of the opponent and not to monitor its own forces. That does not apply to any armed forces in the world and therefore not in the Croatian armed forces either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to get into an argument with you, Admiral, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is Mr. Cayley going to subject himself to cross-examination, Your Honour? He is testifying. It wasn't a question. I ask that his comments be stricken. May I have a ruling, Mr. President? Could I have a ruling on my request to strike his comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The objection is sustained, you're not to make any comments, Mr. Cayley. Just simply put questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is your position of Chief of Military Intelligence in the Croatian armed forces you had no knowledge of the deployment of Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: My task was to monitor, exclusively to monitor the forces of the enemy, their deployment, their intentions. That was my task. My task was not to monitor the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia and least of all the deployment of those forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, simply answer my question "yes" or "no". Is it your testimony that as Chief of Military Intelligence for the Croatian armed forces, you had no knowledge of the deployment of those forces between 1992 and 1994? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I had knowledge about the deployment of enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you're being evasive and I would like an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, I would ask that Mr. Cayley be reprimanded for his comments. He can put a question. He can ask the Court to direct the witness to answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have asked Mr. Cayley not to make any comments. However, I cannot reprimand a counsel for the Prosecution once the answer from the witness is evasive. I have asked Mr. Cayley not to make any comments. However, do not go so far as to request a reprimand. We are before an impasse. I call this an impasse. Mr. Cayley, please avoid making any comment and put questions. The responses then will be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. President, to simply ask the witness to answer "yes" or "no" to my next question, which I think is a fairly straightforward matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That, Mr. President, not if it contradicts the ruling of the Court. The Court told the witness how he should respond to this line. And it may not be possible within the framework that the Court has established to answer yes or no. I would have that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness shall answer as he wishes, as I say, and it's up to the judges to then evaluate his response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I will ask you the question once again. And I would like you to answer me "yes" or "no". As Chief of Military Intelligence, within the Croatian armed forces, are you stating to this Court that you had no knowledge of the deployment of Croatian armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has at least three times answered the same question. This, to me, looks like cross-examination in poor crime films.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you asked for comments not to be made, I don't want you to make comments either. The witness has voluntarily come to this format of questions and response. I have asked Mr. Cayley to ask some questions one at a time. The witness has the right to answer the questions as he sees fit. Please go on, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to keep repeating myself, Admiral. You heard the question, can you give an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have answered that question. As Chief of Intelligence, my task was to monitor, to evaluate the enemy forces and not the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, while you were in Livno, were you a member of the HV or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: My stay in Livno was merely to indicate the importance of defence and what could happen, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you didn't answer my question. I asked you, when you were in Livno, were you a member of the HV or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was there simply to draw attention to the importance of defending the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask, Mr. President, the Court draws the necessary inference from the fact that the witness is simply not answering any of my questions at all. Am I right in saying, Admiral, at the end of May, 1994, you were promoted by President Tudjman to Rear-Admiral?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The rank of Admiral in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I am right in saying that at the same time, Slobodan Praljak was promoted to Reserve Colonel General in the HV and Ante Gotovina to a Major General in the HV. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this question -- Mr. President, this question about Praljak and Gotovina is absolutely outside the focus of examination-in-chief, quite outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Nobilo, but they were questions which were indeed in the scope of the examination-in-chief. I don't know exactly where we are going, but when he answers questions within the framework of the cross-examination, but when he tells us, for example, that he cannot answer questions because he does not have authorisation from the Defence Minister, then that does indeed limit the scope of the examination. But, please, let us reflect again on the text. Their right to refuse to respond. These are rights which are included in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So I don't know what you think of this, Mr. Nobilo, but they are indeed included in these Rules. But it is stated here that it is quite possible that we may use Rule 98, in which case we may then proceed with a further examination of this witness by an official from Croatia in order to obtain any additional information. There is this rule, do not forget. Very well, under these conditions, Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am right in saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that the transcript in English has given, if I may say so, a different version of what you have just stated. In particular, with regards to the possible hearing of this Chamber by the Minister of Defence. I am not a specialist, but I think, perhaps, you might restate what you have just stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. What I have been satisfied myself with saying is that it is very difficult, Mr. Nobilo, to continue with the cross-examination when the witness is invoking that he does not have authorisation to respond to such and such a question. I would like to remind you once again that the witness is not under the protection of Rule 70 as you have said for other witnesses. It is not something that is in my hands. You have chosen your own strategy. Secondly, Rule 90 (F) states the conditions under which the witness under solemn declaration may testify. Thirdly, Rule 98 states that should the case be -- Rule 98 -- let me look back again to the text to be sure. Rule 98 does indeed state that, if necessary, the Trial Chamber may, in order to get a feel for the weight of the evidence presented by the witness, it may call upon the person under whom he is sheltering his responses as saying that he can only give strategic and not tactical responses. So he may then call upon his superior in order to obtain additional information. So here I am calling upon Rule 98. This may be something you may refer to. This is all that I was stating. I hope the transcript now reflects what I am saying. Is it not being reflected in the transcript Mr. Fourmy? No? I see. Well, I am doing what I can. I hope the interpreters will be very attentive to what I am stating. I cannot repeat myself a third time. Mr. Fourmy please ensure that this is indeed what the transcripts shall reflect. I hope that all the persons listening to me understood what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a brief remark to say. I am sorry to intervene. But the first thing is that it was stated in the transcript that Mr. Nobilio, who was stating what I heard you say, perhaps that should be corrected first of all. The second thing, Mr. President, that you have mentioned the differences between strategy and tactics and not -- this does not appear in the transcript, which, as I said, you can either give a tactic or strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that has nothing to do at all with what I said. Please have this stricken. For the rest, it is fine. Very well. Mr. Nobilo, you may now, if you wish to speak, please go ahead. After that, then we're going to take a recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. I understood what you said. But my objection was that this question is outside the focus of the direct examination. That was the substance of my objection. I know that it is up to the Trial Chamber to rule, but then let the Trial Chamber decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would refer, both my learned friend and the Court to Rule 90 (H), which is the foundation for Mr. Nobilo's position. Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of direct examination and matters affecting the credibility of the witness. 89 (H) -- sorry, 90 (H) is a permissive subsection in that the rule, so it states, that the Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion permit, inquire into additional matters as if on direct examination. My position is simply this: I believe that these questions are within the scope of the examination-in-chief. The good admiral spoke about his career in the Croatian Army. These are related to that. And even if the Court considers that they are not, the Court has the discretion to allow me to ask questions as if it were a direct examination. If the witness particularly, bearing in mind that this witness is being evasive for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. My learned colleague reads the Rule well. But, of course, this Rule did not exist and did not apply during the Prosecution case. This is one of the amendments, Rule 90 (H). How many times in the Prosecution case was the Defence quieted on the grounds that we were outside the scope and told you can try and bring the witness back and put on that evidence in your case. We submit the matter of scope to the Court, but I think there is another issue other than what is the wording of Rule 90 (H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard what you have said, Mr. Hayman. And generally speaking I would like to remind you of two things. First of all, the amendments made to the Rules of Procedure, are applicable immediately except, of course, if they're prejudicial for the accused, as you know. For example, and Rule 73 ter was not applied immediately because we did not apply it to the prosecution in the case of 73 bis. I also remind you that, according to the Rules, that the cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the direct examination, but of course, this is not a strict matter. Don't forget there is also an overall governing rule. Is that the judges, in order to render their final judgement, must have a clear understanding of the subject matter and, therefore, they can bring back the witness on several occasions. If there is a witness who has a superior above him, from whom he does not have the authorisation to give such a testimony, then, in particular, that is of importance. This, indeed, was the issue that was raised by Mr. Nobilo in the very beginning. It does allow for cross-examination on two principles, one principle is that it is true that the judges do not have all of the answers from the Admiral for the reasons that he himself as given. In that case, he would not necessarily be required to come back, but that issue may be raised. Yes, Mr. Hayman, you wish to take the floor. But this is only from the goodwill of the Presiding Judge who does not want to cut the Defence short.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would just note, Mr. President, perhaps to provide some context to this drama, if one may call it that, that the Defence does not contest that HV troops went into south-west -- south western Bosnia in this time period to help keep the route open and defeat the JNA. We agree with that. In fact, the need for that, at the strategic level, was a large part of this witness' testimony. I think what's going on here is the Prosecutor is, in essence, asking questions designed to provoke the witness to have to invoke national security. These questions are like, when is the last time you had a secret meeting and something was discussed that you can't disclose? That is what is going on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. I think we shall interrupt the proceedings on this note and to take a recess and then return. I believe we require a 20 to 25 minutes break. The Chamber stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you stated earlier that your function as Chief of Military Intelligence was to monitor those armed forces which were regarded as the enemy of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, did that include monitoring the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 didn't really exist. In 1993, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were the forces that called themselves the Army of Republika Srpska, the BH army and the HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's return now to what we were speaking about before the break. You confirmed in May of 1994 that you were promoted to rear Admiral by President Tudjman; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time it's correct, isn't it, that Slobodan Praljak was promoted to a Reserve Colonel in the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Colonel General, Reserve Colonel General, yes, General Praljak was promoted, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The promotion was in Zagreb. In Zagreb he was promoted, but the General was promoted as a Reserve General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Admiral, and I'm right in saying that Slobodan Praljak had formerly served as a general in the HVO, that's correct; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the Croatian Defence Council, a general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period was he a general in the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really cannot recall for how long, but I know that he first left the Croatian army and then he went to Bosnia-Herzegovina and was a general of the Croatian Defence Council. I don't know the exact date, but probably for about a year, that is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after his service in the HVO he returned to the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. And he was promoted to the rank of retired general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your service in Livno, Ante Gotovina was your commanding officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: My service in Livno, or rather, I was in Livno to investigate, because we knew from our assessments that that is where the main strike would come, and that is why I was in Livno, to investigate. But classically General Gotovina was not my superior, there was no superiority between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ante Gotovina in Livno in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time was he in the HVO or the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: General Gotovina, as he was an experienced officer, at the time was an officer of the Croatian army, because things needed to be organised, because the forces of the Serbs, that is of the JNA, were about to strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript refers to General Kadijevic, I think we're discussing a different person now, just to aid the transcribers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask everyone here present to speak more slowly. I believe it is very difficult for the interpreters to follow such a complex trial; and so, let us all make an effort. In addition, it is true that an error like this one is an important one, even on a phonetic basis it seems to be not at all the same thing; so, let us also try to be more attentive. Please go on, Mr. Cayley, continue. Thank you, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying, Admiral, in May 1998 you were promoted by President Tudjman from the rank of Rear-Admiral to Vice-Admiral; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think at the same time Major General Petkovic was promoted to a Colonel in the HV; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying that Colonel General Milvoj Petkovic was formerly the Chief of Staff of the HVO; is that correct, when he was a brigadier?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: When he was Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In '93, for sure. I think in '94, as well. And I think it was from 1992 he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. And prior to his service as the Chief of Staff of the HVO, he had been an officer in the HV; hadn't he?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that in April of 1992 General Bobetko of the Croatian army was the commander of the southern front?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that command included tactical command of HVO units in Bosnia-Herzegovina; didn't it, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: That command had the role of organising defence in that area, to organise the defence so as to be able to effectively defend that territory because of the closing of the pincers, that was his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, and we have almost finished, but I would like a direct answer to my question. General Bobetko, a Croatian general in the HV, had tactical command of HVO units in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time as part of his command; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have the time frame in the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From at least April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If counsel could close the time frame. Does he mean until 1996, or from a particular month to a particular month? Otherwise, it's vague as to time, that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be allowed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If it could be specified so it is no longer vague, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley, please specify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, in April of 1992 did General Bobetko have command of HVO units in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is how it was called, there was an advanced command post. And that post is not a classical command post, and its role was, as far as I can remember, the organisation of the defence and the forces to close those pincers. So, it was not a classical command function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Bobetko have HVO forces under his command?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: He coordinated and guided those forces in the command to organise themselves. Through this command post he channelled the forces for defence, for defence from this advance command post. In that sense he had a command function, not in the classical sense of command over units below him, but just to distribute those forces and improve their organisation. That was his role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he issue orders to these forces, Admiral, written orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Some, probably he did. Some form of written orders, I assume he had to issue. I think he did have to issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, Admiral, where those written orders are maintained or kept, the archive?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Written orders, every commander keeps them in the archive of the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that archive located, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The archive, if you are referring to the command of General Bobetko, the archive was in Ploca, which is a place in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those orders are still maintained there now?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Those orders are kept in the place where the command for that area was based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, those orders are still in Ploca?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: That I don't know, I don't know where those orders are. I really do not know, but they should be in a command post there in the south. At present the command of the southern Croatian forces is not in Ploca but in Ston, or that is Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President, if I could ask for admission into evidence for exhibit, if the registrar will give me a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With the Court's permission. Before I ask our witness some questions, my proposal would be that all this time be deducted from the Defence time, because it was totally outside the focus of the direct examination which had to do exclusively with strategy. Archives, promotions, these are all additional information that were not covered by the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I speak? This Tribunal, you judges have a truth finding mission, and the Admiral has information and evidence which is relevant to this case. There is discretion within the rules that I have already mentioned which allows me to ask questions. The reason that this cross-examination has taken perhaps longer than it should have done is because the witness has not answered my questions. This time should be deducted from the Defence, they called the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues. The Chamber and the judges have taken the following decision. It calls upon various principles of different types. What has guided the Prosecution is the first principle, is the consequences of the silence of the witness; therefore, it was necessary for the Prosecution to ask indirect questions to try to obtain some of the reality that the Prosecution is pursuing in its objective. Secondly, it is no less true that in the absolute value, the questions that have been put for about half an hour by the Prosecution are outside of the scope of the examination-in-chief. Thirdly, the Trial Chamber has not interrupted the Prosecution, nor will it do so, because the Chamber finds that in its sovereign power, which is its own, to determine what is the truth in the matter referred to it, we will go to the very depth of the question put to the witness by the Prosecution. For that reason it would not be altogether fair for the Defence to suffer the prejudices of the questions put by the Prosecution; therefore, for that reason, 30 minutes in addition will be allotted to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, let's try and demystify some things, if by some strange fact we could call your Defence Minister and ask him to send a fax complying, to tell the Chamber what troops, where and when were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for how long; could you now, according to your recollections, tell that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, if a decision of that kind were to be made I would quite simply not be in a position to say which troops or elements were deployed in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this point in time. This would require additional research, because at the time, quite honestly, I was performing a function which, whose competency was not the deployment of Croatian troops. What was under my authorisation was strategic research as to how that process would develop and evolve, so I could not give an answer of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Admiral, while you performed the duty of head of the Intelligence Department of the Croatian army, did you treat the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an enemy? Did you act, you as an intelligence commander, towards the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or as an intelligence officer of the Croatian army, did you look at the insurgent Krajina regions in the Yugoslav People's Army as a realistic threat? What did you do in your job in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As in the strategy of the defence of the Republic of Croatia, in which I participated myself, there are three basic principles; and one is that Croatia is not considered the enemy of anybody and is not hostile to anyone. That means that my field of activity as the head of the intelligence service was exclusively geared towards the Serbs who were at that time the threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The BH army, in no event, was an enemy of any kind, it was not a threat to Croatia. Therefore, it did not come under the duties of my duties and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, it was only geared towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us throw some more light on the southern front of General Bobetko. I will try and go further from the Prosecutor, and if I enter the realms of state secrets, please do your duty. Therefore, let's proceed. Could General Bobetko liberate and defend the southern part of Croatia without entering the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, because of the small operative depth, General Bobetko could not defend the southern regions of Croatia, that is without doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With his separate command in Bosnia-Herzegovina, his advance command, yes, exactly. And where was the Croatian army active? Which region? Can you show us on the map, using the map, please? How deep did it penetrate into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what was the military reason for this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of this fact, I can assess the depth to which certain elements of the Croatian army could penetrate on the basis of the plan and disposition of the Serb onslaught. And, Your Honours, I would show this now. Therefore, in my assessment as a military analyst, elements of the Croatian army could have entered to a maximum depth the borders of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina on the northern part of the town of Livno. Ultimately up to Tomislavgrad, that is the end point, this line here, because the area of the main onslaught of Serb forces was the valley of Livensko Polje (Phoen) in order to take over the hydro power plant and to move towards Split and by the Neretva River Valley. And second, on the southern side, which stretches from the borders of the Republic of Croatia and borders Bosnia-Herzegovina up to a depth of Stolovic, located here where the laser pen is pointing. So, in my evaluation, it is this depth, and this depth enabled this defence and to prevent the closing of the pincers and defending the southern part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, tell the Court, please, Admiral, whether you know, are there any legal bases, political bases for the entry of the Croatian army into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think that in 1992 there was an agreement reached between the president of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman. On a joint defence from aggression, the Serb aggression, I think that a document of that kind does exist, and it was probably on the basis of that document that the events took place and General Bobetko was designated to come to command the southern front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Bobetko was positioned with his command in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the spring of 1992 when the fateful battle to save Bosnia-Herzegovina and southern Croatia took place. Can you tell us at that time whether, apart from the formal organisation, whether any organisation and preparation at a high level the forces of local Croats from Herzegovina and local Muslims were being prepared for themselves to be able to close the pincers? Did General Bobetko in this fighting command both the Croats and the Muslims in defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As there are several questions there, let me answer in the following manner. It is quite certainly true that the organisation of Croats in Bosnia was better than the organisation of the Bosnian Muslims in that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as we are dealing with an asymmetrical war where the technical factor is greater on the Serbian side, these forces were absolutely no guarantee, although the Croats were better organised. But, it is also a fact that in addition to the Croats in the units which were commanded by General Bobetko, there were also units of Bosnian Muslims, and this was simultaneous, they existed at the same time, and I am certain that I stressed this in my presentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, General Praljak, is he a native of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Petkovic was from Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Petkovic, his origins are from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he lived in Sibenik, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that at beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina a group of officers and soldiers from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who originated from BH and who took part in the Croatian army during the Serbo-Croat War, asked to step down from the Croatian army so as to be able to go home and defend their own home in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were instances of this kind, some Croats who were in the Croatian army after January, 1992, not quite then, but somewhere in the second half of March and the beginning of April asked to go to Herzegovina, to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, we have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Your Honour, as I have explained to you, you will now have questions put to you by the judges for the completion of your testimony here before this Tribunal. I now turn to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, to the President. Microphone to the Judge Riad, please. Microphone to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have listened very attentively to your testimony and your presentation on military strategy. It seems that you are a great expert on this subject. However, I cannot say that I was able to assimilate everything at once. I must look at the transcript once again to learn more. But I concluded from that that the fundamental responsibility for all that occurred of all those events, that the responsibility was attributed to the Serbs. I would just like to ask you questions dealing more, more relative, whether it deals more directly with our trial, but I am going to tempt myself with general questions, dealing again with your testimony. If I understood correctly, do you consider that the Serbs are responsible for the confrontation, which took place between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia? Do you believe that they are the cause or, rather, who was the cause for this confrontation? Because the two had a common enemy. If you will respond to that question, you will help me or help us to follow and to understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I have understood your question correctly, it is whether the Serbs were the cause of the confrontation between the Bosnia Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Have I understood your question correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In other words, what was the cause?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to my research, which I have spoken about from the elements of strategy, I came to the conclusion, and this can be seen from the map, the situation is as such: It is 1993, the year 1993. The main objective cause in strategy, this is called the external circle. The external circle is much more decisive and influential for events within the circle itself than what is actually taking place in the epicentre. This means in practical terms the following: That on a strategic level, on the aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this phenomenon stepped into play. That is to say, the Serbs pushed at the same time both the Bosnian Muslims and Croats, into that circle. And by applying the strategy of real threat, realistic threat, they created a psychosis. This psychosis, the longer it lasted, objectively gave birth to the confrontation between the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. Therefore, my conclusion, Your Honours, and I think that this is what my research has shown, that it was a basic cause for that confrontation. This also bears out one other thing. Because the Serbs had already used up a portion of their forces, they could no longer effect a global offensive. And by applying this strategy, they quite simply waited, lay in waiting. We can compare this to the strategy of a spider with his web waiting for his prey to be caught. And this, at the same time, is meant by the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. And that, Your Honours, is the external circle in the area of strategy of how you can liquidate your enemy. And I think that that in this case is the principal cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You gave a very interesting example when you compared that to the battle between elephants. Is there any particular reason, the specific reason that the Bosnia Croats fought against the Muslims? You stated that the Croats were better organised than the Muslims, the Bosnian Muslims. And that the Bosnian Muslims never posed any real threat to the Croats. So what is the reason then for the Croats to want to get rid of the Muslims? And there was also ascensions, that you said and I read this from the transcripts, so I am going to read it for you in English. By wavering has strengthened the conviction by the JNA that the war would end quickly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, that sentence, I think was contained in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Let me continue now. I would like to repeat because I don't think it was translated correctly from French. Mr. President, perhaps you have understood the translation. I must admit I don't follow the French translation very well. I followed the translation into French, so I will repeat the question. It seems one part of the Bosnian Muslim leaders, they're wavering and this to enforce the convictions among the JNA that this battle could be won quickly. Do you feel that this would also encourage the Croatian Army, this give them -- do you think that there was some sort of agreement that agreed between the two sides, the Muslims and the Serbs, because that's why the -- because you said at one point that they had begun to abdicate their forces.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be happy to try and explain the situation. I think there is a nuance of interpretation here because strategy has its nuances as well. Let's see what we're talking about. As the plan that you have seen is a very complex plan, a very sophisticated plan by which they wish to achieve a greater Serbia, many people, even in the Republic of Croatia, were certain that a war of this kind would actually break out. At the same time, some people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not certain that war was imminent. It is possible, Your Honours, that a portion of the Bosnian Muslim leadership thought only at the beginning, at the very beginnings of the war, that is to say the beginning of 1992, that they would avoid an aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina in that way. And in view of the defensive strategic interests, this cannot be considered to have been a bad thing. And this meant that if as the Serbs had the enormous advantage, and where we were talking about time here, it was a question of time, Your Honours, one month, perhaps, 15 days, were in question because it was April 1992 and any hesitation in decision, any lack of a fast reaction, could have brought what you saw happen here. So we cannot explicitly state that the Bosnian Muslims and their leadership did not wish to do so. At that moment they did not, perhaps, have a full understanding of the situation. But subsequent events were to show that after the pincers were stopped, prevented in closing, they came to realise in the political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the Bosnian Muslim leadership, that aggression was there and they then began to organise themselves, the armed forces and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina began to organise itself. And, in that sense, that is the right observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, very well. That is not the reason for the conflict, I understand. You also talked about the agents of the Croatian forces in order to secure the Croatian territories. You said that during the examination by the Defence. Now, these Croatian forces who entered, did they come into contact or into the battles with the Bosnian forces? Were there any battles between the Bosnian forces and the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are talking about 1992. The first phase of the war in closing the pincers and that is the key point. At that time, there were no conflicts between the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina existed and the Bosnian Muslims. On the contrary, at that time, and I am talking about Bosnia Muslims as opposed to the other regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they became included and they joined forces to the best of their ability, to prevent the pincers. So, at that time, there were no conflicts between the Croats and the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question to wind up and over which I have some difficulty understanding. You said that there was a total lack of equality of balance between the Serbian forces, the Croatian forces and the Bosnian forces. You said regarding the Croats it was 1-10. And in the case of the Bosniaks, it was 1-1.000 because these were armed forces against non-armed forces, non-armed people. The United Nations, as far as I remembered, prohibited delivery of weapons, so how come the Serbs were so strong in spite of the ban on arm supply? Why was there this ban when there was such a large disproportion? You're a military expert, could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as a man and a general, the question that I have just heard is a question above all questions when we're talking about the events in the former Yugoslavia. It is a question upon which many in the future will have to find an answer to and will have to dwell on. But on the basis of my research, I can say the following, and that is why I said in my introductory testimony, I use the term asymmetrical war. Here, that is to say, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, an asymmetric war was waged. An asymmetrical war could have been waged only on one condition and that is the embargo.
