As in 1985 and 6 and 7, a Serbian imperial force was organised which wanted to emerge on the western borders and take away portions of Croatia and the entire region of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This asymmetric war led to the fact that in those regions, as so many victims fell and a complete chaos reigned. And I would like before Your Honours, to say that this strategic game and to call it a determined chaos. But, at the same time, before Your Honours, as an officer and an admiral, I have great satisfaction in seeing that we succeeded in maintaining Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state. And in the first phase of the war, in setting up a joint defence, as well as in the second phase of the war, to have a joint attack. And that the international forces ensured the entirety of Bosnia. This also means that we have a whole Croatia. Why and for what reason an asymmetric war was allowed to take place and the City of Sarajevo to be destroyed for three years before the eyes of the world, Your Honours, that is something that will have to be studied in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. I turn to Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Admiral, I also have listened to your testimony with much interest. Let me start off with a little question about the Serbian Academy of Sciences. You mentioned the Academy. I am a little unclear in my mind about the precise status of the Academy. Was the Academy regarded as a spokesman of the Government of Serbia on the matters to which you refer?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have understood your question, Your Honour. I did not deal with this in the sense of the structure of the Serbian Academy of Science. But, I shall tell you what I personally know from my general education. As far as I know, the Serbian Academy of Science, like any other academy of science, should promote scientific work in certain fields. Among others, social phenomenon, international relations and so on and so forth, the natural sciences, technology and so forth. However, the Serbian Academy of Science was not an instrument of the Government of Serbia. It was not an instrument of the Presidency of Serbia. Like any other academy of science, it was an independent institution. However, in the Serbian Academy of Science, according to the structure of the academicians members of the academy within it, they were exclusively from the social humanitarian sciences. And they had authority and the power to determine in the sense of scientific research, what is good and what is bad for the Serbs as a whole, as an entity, both through their scientific authority as scientists, men of science. The results of their endeavours resulted in a memorandum in 1986. That authority, scientific authority for the Serbs was binding. And, for them, it meant absolute truth. That absolute truth was put forward by the names of academicians and the loftiest academic institutions. So 1986 was the year when the armed forces, that is to say, the JNA, had started its reorganisation and had become a Serbian, imperial force. That component, along with the component of the memorandum as an ideological platform, offered the political structure, as a legitimacy too as a guiding light and to exert pressure on to federal aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That the conclusions reached by the Serbian academy of sciences were regarded as corresponding to the positions of the Government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you a very little question about Lieutenant General Gavric. I may not be pronouncing the name correctly and I hope to be forgiven. I thought you said that he was in captivity in Sarajevo. Is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was General Kukanjac, he was in captivity. That is to say, at that particular time, and we're talking about the 10th of May, 1992, when the attack on Sarajevo started, when the whole city was exposed to fire, the only thing that was important was to reach the main commander, to prevent this destruction. At that time, this meant salvation for Sarajevo as a city. But an answer to this operation by the Serbs was to appoint General Mladic as commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So why was the General in captivity? To prevent what?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The destruction of Sarajevo. It was a Serb general. He was the commander. And the Bosniaks, the inhabitants of Sarajevo succeeded in circling him and captured him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Now I understand a little more clearly. Now, you would have heard learned counsel, Mr. Hayman, say something like this and if I have got him wrong, he would correct me immediately, I know. That the Defence in this case is not contesting that HV forces were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their Defence rests on other positions. Do you confirm his statement, that HV forces were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, according to my evaluation, I don't know which units, because I did not go into that, I truly don't know. But that some elements of the armed forces, of the Croatian Army were, according to my assessment as an analyst, I said the depth to which this could have been the depth in my assessment from the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the Town of Tomislavgrad. That is a depth of about 15 to 20 kilometres and the same thing in the south, which means yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let me, in this connection, recall that part of your testimony in which you referred to an agreement between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic for HV forces to serve in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, an agreement did exist between the president of the presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and the President of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman on a joint defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, it existed, as far as I know. Its exact contact I don't know. But I do know that an agreement of that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I accept what you say that you haven't got a ready recollection or grasp of its exact contents. But would you know, generally, whether that agreement between the two presidents authorised HV officers to serve in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: There was no competence in that sense to serve in the HVO, not in that sense. It wasn't binding in that sense as far as I know. But, exclusively, that is the fact that Croats left the Croatian Army in that first phase of the war, this was on a voluntary basis, so they left voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now let's talk about HV officers who left on a voluntary basis to serve in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were HV officers in Croatia, would they have had to get official approval to leave the HV in Croatia to go over into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, they would need official permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What would be the status of their service in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would they be regarded by the Croatian authorities as serving on secondment in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, they were temporarily assigned there to prevent a disaster. One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: While in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what would happen with their pay from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that they must have received their pay from Croatia because there was no one to pay them in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then would I be right, Admiral, in supposing that at the end of their service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they would have had an automatic right of reversion to the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Those of them who wanted to return, could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the directive of the defence minister, which authorised you to testify only on certain matters. Would I be right in thinking that what you were saying was that if you testified on those matters, not only would you be violating his directive, but that the violation would constitute a criminal offence under the law of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: It would constitute a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about standard military practices. You remember that during one phase of your evidence, you referred to a certain practice -- I don't rightly recall exactly what it was -- being a standard military practice in the armed forces of all countries in the world. Do you remember saying something like that? That you were talking about a standard military practice?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you, Admiral, say that it is a standard military practice world-wide for the Chief of Military Intelligence over an army to know of the global deployment of the main elements of that army?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The global deployment at the highest level, one might know. Because the global level is the area of strategy, but the Chief of Intelligence, I don't know expressly because this, after all, is the top secret of any armed force in the world for him to deal with the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now we are making progress very rapidly, I see. Let's talk about the position of Serbia in all of these matters. I gather you concur with Judge Riad's summary, which I share, that your evidence was to the effect that the conflict between Croatia and the Muslims was due to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, a military officer would, I take it, and this is just while theorising on my part, because I am not a military man, have been trained in some kind of capacity to empathise, to see the thing from a point of view of the other man, so as to acquire objectivity. Suppose we had before us today, a Serbian admiral, do you think he would accept your proposition that the conflict between the Croatians and the Muslims was entirely attributable to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Probably, Your Honour, that would depend on the admiral in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Of course it would.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I say that, I am referring to the depth of his studies. Would he view this problem from the strategic level or at a lower level? My assumption is, that depends on the individual, his education, his background, his understanding for strategy. But in the scientific way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Suppose he was a cultivated and learned gentleman like yourself, would you think that he would accept your version?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for the compliment. But if he were indeed such, and if he were to apply scientific criteria of warfare, then I think he would come to the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn to this distinction between the strategic and the tactical. Would I be right, Admiral, in supposing that there is a grey area within which the two concepts tended to merge?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In military circles even, there is confusion often between the tactical and the strategic. And I will tell you what the NATO standard is. Tactics is exclusively, and I stress exclusively, devoted to the way in which a certain piece of equipment or a unit should be used in a particular battle. So this is purely military operations; whereas at the level of strategy, that does not, especially not in war, refer to the use of military effectiveness. Because in addition to the military resources, there are others. In theory, which is generally accepted by Beaufour, the French military theoretician, who said that a war is waged at the level of general strategy. And general strategy comprises military strategy, political strategy, diplomatic strategy, cultural strategy. And, Your Honours, most recently because we are living in the post-modern era, information strategy too. And by combining those strategy a war is waged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Admiral, I am grateful and I see I have entered into an area in which I needed to be educated. Thank you very much. Now let us talk a little bit about it this way. Supposing there was an agreement between President Tudjman and President Milosevic for the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, supposing, would you regard that as pertaining to strategy or to tactics?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Exclusively strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would I be right in thinking that the strategy of a nation could itself evolve over time, it could change its components?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As opposed to tactics, which can change very easily. Strategy, at least it should not change so often. But even if any changes do occur, those changes have to be minor, of a corrective nature, in the sense of a correction rather than a global change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But you have already said that if there was a presidential agreement to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina that would pertain the strategy.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What do you think of this proposition, suppose, according to you, it was said that the strategy of the Serbs was to absorb the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and suppose you added to that a subsequent agreement of the kind I mentioned; would it follow that the original strategy had become modified, that a strategy of total absorption had become modified by a strategy of partition?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think you could make such a conclusion. It would be possible, but under one hypothetical condition, and that is if there had not been the war in Croatia. And since there had been a bloody, destructive war, then this hypothesis does not stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Admiral, did there ever come a time when the Serbs were prepared to accept less than the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and give the balance to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: To understand the question better, what exactly do you mean by balancing the situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, there must be a translation problem. I didn't speak about balancing the situation. What I asked was: Did there ever come a time when the Serbs were prepared to accept less than the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to give the remainder to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that such a situation did not occur, and that it was not present on the Serb side. Why is it that I can claim this, even though this would require additional research? For the reason that the occupied parts of the Republic of Croatia were retained and the occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Serbs covered 70 per cent. So, I assume that is the situation you're referring to. But even then, that is not the map that we see here from 1993. The Serbs always thought that some kind of favourable environment, political environment would set in for them to take as much of Bosnia as they could, preferably the whole. A rapid analysis that comes to my mind is that the strategy of constant threat meant that even Dubrovnik was exposed to artillery fire up to '95. This was an indicator that they had not given up their ideas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a slightly different question. Did there ever come a time when the Serbs were cooperating with the Croatians in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: With the Croats? You mean the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That is the Bosnian Croats or the Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Croatian Croatians.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Military forces.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: There was never any such cooperation in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us go finally to this article, I didn't retain the numbering of it. I wonder if colleagues could help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: 466, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: 466; do you remember, Admiral, this Exhibit 466?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And page 8 you were reading something, and I didn't take a note at the time, at the top left-hand column. Would you like to read those words again? Could you read them and the translator would translate them for me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: "Since the efforts of the JNA for Bosnia to fall quickly, the threat and selective use of force did not produce results, primarily among the Croatian people who had organised themselves militarily. So, it focused on the concrete implementation of the pacification of Bosnia-Herzegovina, modelled on the Croatian example. Because the Bosnian Muslim section of the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by its hesitation, had increased the conviction of the JNA that the war would end quickly".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I invite you, Admiral, to focus on the word pacification? Now, is the use of that word in your discipline more proximate to the idea of more conquering or protecting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: The way I use it, it is closer to occupation, capture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Admiral, you have been a great help to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was an honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Admiral, I'm not going to take too long and extend the debate any further, which is already long, I shall just follow on to what Judge Shahabuddeen just said, you answered very well many of the questions that I myself was asking myself and which were asked by Judge Shahabuddeen and Judge Riad. Let us go on with a few clarifications. I see there's an apparent change of attitude which I find most acceptable because, thanks to you, I have better understood the difference between the word strategy and tactics. I was able to understand that when you refused to answer this was more of a strategy, and when you agreed to answer, this could be described as tactics. So, thank you for the second concept winning over. I just need one or two points to be clarified, Admiral. And then we will adjourn. In the agreement that Judge Shahabuddeen has just referred to, this agreement on joint defence between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your opinion, in view of the position you held, in your mind, Mr. Izetbegovic and the high political and military leaders, were they in agreement to apply just then, the period we're interested in, to implement that agreement? Was this relayed by the media? Do you understand my question? Or on the contrary, when the Croatian forces pledged themselves at the disposal of the HVO one just said, "We are entitled to do this because there was an agreement"? There is a slight shade of meaning, different meaning between the two. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have to go back to strategy once again. Since in the overall strategy of warfare, in view of the level of development of civilisation in the third revolution, that is the era of information, that information is important and at times decisive. I must note that in those days it was not sufficiently developed on either the Croatian or the Bosnian side for such a special strategy to be applied. As far as I can recall, it was not fully utilised and it was not sufficiently presented to the public, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You haven't quite understood my questions. I don't know whether that is strategy or tactics. But what I wanted to know, simply, was whether in this kind of partial occupation of, on the part of Croatia in Bosnia, central Bosnia, whether at any given moment in the course of developments you had the impression that Izetbegovic and the Muslim forces said let us implement this agreement so that we should become militarily stronger. That is all I'm asking you. Because there was an agreement, I'm asking whether in the course of developments itself it was invoked not just by one side of Croatia, but by both, because if there was an agreement, you will agree it must be between two sides. That was my question. Perhaps you can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm trying to, I do apologise, Mr. President, if I did not understand your question completely. But I shall do my best to try and answer it. Have I understood you well, since there was this agreement, your question is, Mr. President, whether it was implemented, and to what extent by the Bosnian leadership? Did it take advantage of that agreement, did it place emphasis on it? Have I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, because I understood that the Croatian leaders did rely on it. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: In my opinion they didn't use it sufficiently, in my opinion. I'm trying to recall, maybe they could have done better, and it may have been more useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. I have a last question to put to you. The accused is here, Colonel Blaskic, at the time, I didn't quite understand the chain of superior command. In other words, who was in command over Colonel Blaskic? And was this command linked to the Croatian forces? Was it General Bobetko, was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Blaskic was not within the chain of command linked to General Bobetko. General Blaskic was the commander of an operative zone, the operative zone of central Bosnia. And according to the vertical chain of command, he came under the command of the main command of the HVO. That is the line of command, the line of subordination in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And according to you it was at that level that he communicated with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: At what level do you mean? At the level of the operative zone or at the level of the main command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The operative zone depended on a headquarters, you have just said that. And I'm asking whether at the level of the headquarters there was a military tactical strategic link with the Croatian forces, or at least with the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since this was an area that is the gateway which was of key significance for defence, it is quite possible that there may have been cooperation in the sense of coordination rather than command. The expression coordination means the coordination of the activities of each in his own area, so as to ensure the best possible defence, so the form of coordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But these relations did exist, then, those relations existed, these relations of coordination?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, in the shape of coordination, but not command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But in times of war you will agree with me, coordination is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is important. Coordination means that the forces in this area should carry out their assignments, and that the forces in this area should carry out their assignments. Because there was a constant threat of the renewed operations of the enemy and the closing of these pincers, there is a fundamental difference between coordination and command in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, Admiral, all that remains for me to do is to thank you, but I noted a question from the Prosecutor when you were able to answer where certain archives were, and I think the Prosecutor can get that information from another source; but I would like to thank you by calling on countries, yours and all others through your example, for total loyal and wholehearted cooperation with this Tribunal. This Tribunal is not composed of judges who pretend to be judges, they have been mandated by the Security Council within the framework of a statute and in mind with very lofty international standards. The Tribunal has the tools to firmly require of all states concerned better cooperation, and that is in the first place in the interest of the person here, the accused, and it is the duty of all of us. Admiral, thank you for coming here, this was lengthy, but I think it was useful. Now, the registrar, unless Mr. Nobilo has a question, is to tender exhibits, I assume. You have a question to put, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. A very minor detail. As the accused is a party to this trial, he sent me a message that there was an error in the transcript. When the Admiral was listing the armies who constituted the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Admiral mentioned the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of Republika Srpska and the HVO, and what appears in the transcript is HV. So could this fact be noted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, I think Mr. Registrar, we have to pay the greatest attention to this transcript, we have a lot of problems, far be it for me to criticise our interpreters who have an extremely difficult task; but the transcript is very important because we have to use it and rely on it 100 per cent. Let me remind everyone that we are meeting tomorrow at 9.45 with two breaks. It is a quarter to 6.00, I thank the interpreters and we meet again tomorrow at 9.45. This hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.53 p.m., to be reconvened on the 11th day of September, 1998, at 9.45 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
